bio.body.cancer.the-fifth-power-of-your-.title: Cancer incidence rises as about the fifth power of your age
bio.body.cancer.the-fifth-power-of-your-.hook: Plot cancer incidence against age on log paper and you get a straight line of slope five. That slope is a count of something.
bio.body.cancer.the-fifth-power-of-your-.author: author-bio-1

reviewed.notes: Source was misattributed: the 2007 Lancet Oncology "Armitage and Doll revisited" paper is by Hornsby, Page and Tomlinson, not by Armitage and Doll. Fixed author and citation.

bio.body.cancer.the-fifth-power-of-your-.body:
Take the incidence of colon, stomach or pancreatic cancer, plot it against age with both axes logarithmic, and you get a straight line with a slope of roughly five or six. That is a strange shape. If cancer were simple accumulating wear, incidence would climb roughly in proportion to age — slope one. A fifth power is the fingerprint of something that requires several independent rare events to land in the *same* cell.

Armitage and Doll said so in 1954 and read the slope as a count: number of required steps, minus one. Six or seven hits.

Underneath is the part that connects to everything else. Cancer is evolution running inside you, on your time. A cell that mutates into dividing a little faster leaves more descendants, which are the cells most likely to pick up the next mutation. Variation, heredity, differential success — Darwin's three conditions, with your body as the environment and no need for anyone to want the outcome.

The slope is solid. The interpretation is not.
bio.body.cancer.the-fifth-power-of-your-.rigor:
Suppose a cell needs $k$ specific events, each arriving independently at small rate $p_i$ per unit time, in a fixed population of $N$ susceptible cells. The probability that one cell has completed all $k$ in order by time $t$ is approximately $p_1p_2\cdots p_k\,t^{k}/k!$, so the *incidence* — the derivative — is

$$I(t)\;\approx\;N\,\frac{p_1p_2\cdots p_k}{(k-1)!}\;t^{\,k-1}.$$

Take logs: $\log I = (k-1)\log t + \text{const}$. The log–log slope counts the stages minus one, and Armitage and Doll's slopes of 5–6 gave $k\approx 6$–$7$.

Three caveats, all live. Incidence decelerates and often falls above about 80, which this model cannot produce at all. The Moolgavkar–Venzon–Knudson model fits the same curves with only *two* rate-limiting events plus clonal expansion of the intermediate cells — so the exponent does not identify a mutation count. And deep sequencing now finds large driver-mutant clones sitting in morphologically normal skin and oesophagus, meaning "stages" and "driver mutations" are not the same thing.

recall.question: Why does a log–log slope near five argue against cancer being simple accumulated damage?

options.text: Steady damage would give incidence roughly proportional to age, slope one
options.why: a high power means several independent rare events must coincide in one cell.

options.text: Because damage accumulates exponentially, not as a power law
options.why: cumulative damage grows linearly in time; the exponential would be even harder to square with the data.

options.text: Because older people are exposed to more carcinogens
options.why: exposure duration matters, but it cannot by itself bend a linear process into a fifth power.

options.text: Because incidence falls again in the very old
options.why: that flattening is real and is a problem for the multistage model too, not evidence about damage.

sources.title: The Age Distribution of Cancer and a Multi-stage Theory of Carcinogenesis, British Journal of Cancer 8(1), 1–12
sources.author: Peter Armitage and Richard Doll

sources.title: What can we learn from the population incidence of cancer? Armitage and Doll revisited, Lancet Oncology 8(11), 1030–1038
sources.author: Catherine Hornsby, Karen M. Page, Ian P. M. Tomlinson

bio.body.hormones.the-patent-that-cost-a.title: They signed away insulin for a dollar each
bio.body.hormones.the-patent-that-cost-a.hook: Three men signed away the insulin patent for a dollar each. The quote everybody attaches to that story appears to be invented.
bio.body.hormones.the-patent-that-cost-a.author: author-bio-1
bio.body.hormones.the-patent-that-cost-a.body:
In 1921, in a borrowed Toronto laboratory, Frederick Banting and Charles Best pulled something out of dog pancreas that dropped blood sugar. James Collip purified it enough to put into a person. On 11 January 1922 a fourteen-year-old named Leonard Thompson got the first injection; the first batch was too crude and the second worked. Children who had been left in wards to die in diabetic comas woke up.

Banting, Best and Collip assigned the patent to the University of Toronto for one dollar each. The line everyone quotes — that insulin belonged to the world and not to him — is not documented in anything Banting wrote or said; it seems to trace back to a children's biography published in 1959. The patent was also not purely a gift: holding it stopped anyone else from patenting insulin and let Toronto set quality standards for the firms that manufactured it.

What they had found is the cleanest example of a hormone: a molecule built in one organ, poured into the blood, and read by cells across the whole body as a single instruction — take up glucose, now.

recall.question: What makes insulin a textbook example of a hormone?

options.text: It is made in one organ, travels in the blood, and is read as an instruction by cells everywhere that carry its receptor
options.why: action at a distance, chemically addressed.

options.text: It is the only molecule that controls blood sugar
options.why: glucagon, cortisol and adrenaline all move blood sugar too, in the opposite direction.

options.text: It works by entering cells and editing their genes
options.why: it binds a receptor on the cell surface and triggers a signalling cascade inside.

options.text: It is produced only when you eat
options.why: secretion tracks blood glucose continuously, with a low baseline at all times.

sources.title: Did a Scientist Sell the Insulin Patent for \$1? (fact check)

bio.body.immune-system.counting-for-a-li.title: Remember counting arrangements? Your immune system does it for a living
bio.body.immune-system.counting-for-a-li.hook: A few dozen gene segments, cut and pasted at random, generate more receptor shapes than there are cells in your body.
bio.body.immune-system.counting-for-a-li.author: author-bio-1
bio.body.immune-system.counting-for-a-li.body:
Counting taught you that a short ingredient list generates a catalogue nobody could ever write out. Your immune system is that fact, implemented in flesh, under a deadline.

The problem: you will meet pathogens that have never existed before, so you cannot carry a gene for each. The solution is to stop storing and start generating. As each B cell develops, it physically cuts its own DNA and splices together one segment from each of three small libraries, then chews back the ends and inserts random letters at the joins. Every lymphocyte finishes with a different receptor, and none of them was designed for anything.

Then the second half, which is pure selection. Cells that bind your own tissues are killed off. A cell that binds something real is told to divide, and its descendants mutate the receptor further and are re-selected for tighter binding. Burnet named this clonal selection in 1957; Tonegawa showed in 1976 that the DNA really is being cut and re-joined.

Here is the accounting.
bio.body.immune-system.counting-for-a-li.rigor:
The human immunoglobulin heavy-chain locus holds roughly 44 V, 27 D and 6 J segments. Pure choice gives

$$44\times27\times6\approx7\times10^{3}$$

heavy chains, multiplied again by the light chain's own combinations. That alone is unimpressive. The explosion comes from the joins: nucleotides are trimmed and added at random where the segments meet, so the junction itself is a variable-length random string. Textbook estimates of the potential repertoire land near $10^{12}$–$10^{13}$; sequencing-based estimators push the bound on paired sequences far higher, and the spread between methods is several orders of magnitude, so treat any single figure with suspicion.

Against that, the *realised* repertoire in one person is on the order of $10^{7}$–$10^{9}$ distinct clones. You never hold the catalogue. You hold a random sample of it, vanishingly small, and rely on receptors being sloppy enough that near-misses still bind.

Then comes hill-climbing. Somatic hypermutation runs at about $10^{-3}$ per base per division in the receptor genes — roughly a million times the background rate — and selection keeps the best binders each round. Generate broadly, sample thinly, then optimise locally: the same three-step shape as evolution, compressed into a fortnight.

recall.question: Why can't your body simply store a gene for every antibody it might need?

options.text: The potential repertoire is astronomically larger than the genome
options.why: the only way to cover it is to generate receptors combinatorially and sample, not to store them.

options.text: Because antibodies are proteins and proteins cannot be encoded
options.why: every antibody *is* encoded by a gene; the point is how many distinct genes would be required.

options.text: Because pathogens mutate too quickly to be catalogued
options.why: they do, but the deeper problem is the size of the space before anything mutates.

options.text: Because the genes would take too long to transcribe
options.why: transcription speed is irrelevant; storage capacity is the binding constraint.

sources.title: Commonality despite exceptional diversity in the baseline human antibody repertoire, Nature 566, 393–397
sources.author: Bryan Briney, Anne Inderbitzin, Collin Joyce, Dennis R. Burton

bio.body.microbiome.not-outnumbered-ten-.title: You are not outnumbered ten to one
bio.body.microbiome.not-outnumbered-ten-.hook: "Ten bacterial cells for every human cell" was a back-of-envelope guess from 1972 that ran unchallenged for forty years.
bio.body.microbiome.not-outnumbered-ten-.author: author-bio-1
bio.body.microbiome.not-outnumbered-ten-.body: The claim that bacteria outnumber your own cells ten to one came from a rough estimate published in 1972, and got repeated for four decades because it is a lovely thing to say. In 2016 Sender, Fuchs and Milo did the arithmetic properly for a 70 kg reference man: about 3.8 × 10¹³ bacteria against about 3.0 × 10¹³ human cells. The real ratio is close to one to one — and a single visit to the bathroom shifts it.

recall.question: What is the actual ratio of bacterial to human cells in the body, and why did the old number survive so long?
recall.answer: Roughly 1.3 to 1, not 10 to 1 — about 3.8 × 10¹³ bacteria to 3.0 × 10¹³ human cells (Sender, Fuchs and Milo, 2016). The old figure was a rough 1972 estimate that nobody rechecked, because it was memorable, repeatable and flattering to the field.

sources.title: Revised Estimates for the Number of Human and Bacteria Cells in the Body, PLOS Biology 14(8), e1002533
sources.author: Ron Sender, Shai Fuchs, Ron Milo

bio.body.viruses.the-blender-experiment.title: The kitchen blender that proved genes are made of DNA
bio.body.viruses.the-blender-experiment.hook: A kitchen blender and two radioactive labels finally ended an argument the field had been refusing to settle for eight years.
bio.body.viruses.the-blender-experiment.author: author-bio-1

reviewed.notes: Added the Avery 1944 caveat — Hershey-Chase persuaded the field rather than settling the question from scratch.

bio.body.viruses.the-blender-experiment.body:
In 1952 most biologists still expected genes to be protein. Proteins have twenty kinds of building block and DNA has four; four letters looked too dull to write an organism. Avery and colleagues had shown otherwise in 1944; the field shrugged.

Alfred Hershey and Martha Chase made it stick, with a Waring blender. They grew bacteriophages — viruses that hunt bacteria — in two batches. One batch was fed radioactive sulphur, which goes into protein and not into DNA. The other got radioactive phosphorus, which goes into DNA and not into protein. Then they let each batch of phages latch onto *E. coli* and ran the mixture in the blender, which shears off anything still stuck to the outside of a cell.

The sulphur stayed outside. The phosphorus went in, and the infected cells went on to make new phages. Whatever carries the instructions had entered the bacterium, and it was not the protein.

The experiment works because of what a virus is: a protein container with a genome inside and a mechanism for injecting it. The box waits on the doorstep. The instructions go in and take over the kitchen.

recall.question: Why was the blender the crucial piece of equipment?

options.text: It sheared the phage coats off the outside of the bacteria
options.why: only then could the two labels be sorted into "went in" and "stayed out".

options.text: It mixed the phages with the bacteria so infection could occur
options.why: infection happens on its own; the blender was used afterwards.

options.text: It broke the bacteria open to release their contents
options.why: breaking the cells would have mixed everything together and destroyed the comparison.

options.text: It separated DNA from protein inside the phage
options.why: the two labels were already in different molecules; the blender separated inside from outside.

sources.title: Independent Functions of Viral Protein and Nucleic Acid in Growth of Bacteriophage, Journal of General Physiology 36, 39–56
sources.author: A. D. Hershey and Martha Chase

bio.cells.division.two-metres-no-knots.title: Two metres of thread in a six-micron room, and it never knots
bio.cells.division.two-metres-no-knots.hook: Twenty kilometres of fishing line in a tennis ball — copied and pulled apart without a knot, every time a cell divides.
bio.cells.division.two-metres-no-knots.author: author-bio-1
bio.cells.division.two-metres-no-knots.body:
Stretch the DNA in one of your cells end to end and you get about two metres. It lives inside a nucleus roughly six thousandths of a millimetre across. Scale that up and you have twenty kilometres of fishing line stuffed into a tennis ball. Now copy every centimetre of it and drag the two copies to opposite ends of the room without leaving them linked.

This is a topology problem, and cells solve it with topology tools. Enzymes called topoisomerases cut the double helix, let another strand pass through the gap, and seal it again. Cut, pass, reseal: that is exactly the crossing change a knot theorist draws on paper when simplifying a tangle.

The type II enzymes do the heavy version. They cut both strands of one helix and pass an entire second helix through the hole, which is how two finished chromosomes, wound around each other after copying, finally come apart. Jam those enzymes and division stalls — which is precisely what several chemotherapy drugs are built to do.

recall.question: What does a type II topoisomerase actually do to untangle two chromosomes?

options.text: Cuts both strands of one helix, passes a second helix through the gap, then reseals
options.why: a physical crossing change, the same move that simplifies a knot diagram.

options.text: Pulls the chromosomes apart with a motor until the tangle slips loose
options.why: pulling on a linked pair only tightens it; something has to be cut open.

options.text: Rewrites the tangled stretch of sequence so the knot disappears
options.why: the sequence is never edited; only the crossings change.

bio.cells.energy-atp.the-proton-waterfal.title: Remember that energy is conserved but not free? Cells built a dam
bio.cells.energy-atp.the-proton-waterfal.hook: You already know energy is conserved but not free. Your cells turn that into a dam, a waterfall and a spinning turbine.
bio.cells.energy-atp.the-proton-waterfal.author: author-bio-1

reviewed.notes: Cyanobacteria have no chloroplasts: the c14 ring is the plant chloroplast one. Named the ring sizes (8 and 14) that give the 2.7 and 4.7 ratios.

bio.cells.energy-atp.the-proton-waterfal.body:
The first law says you cannot create energy; the second says you cannot use all of what you have. A cell lives inside both, and its solution is a hydroelectric plant, built to the same plan as the one in Guatapé.

Food gives up electrons. Those electrons fall down a chain of proteins in the inner mitochondrial membrane, and at three points along the fall the proteins use the released energy to shove protons to the far side. Now one side is crowded and positive: a reservoir behind a dam. The only way back is through a turbine. That turbine is ATP synthase, and it genuinely rotates — a stalk spinning inside a ring, driven by protons falling through it, screwing phosphate onto ADP at the top.

An adult recycles something like fifty kilograms of ATP a day, close to a body's worth, out of a standing stock measured in grams. Peter Mitchell proposed this in 1961 and was largely ridiculed for it. He took the Nobel in 1978.
bio.cells.energy-atp.the-proton-waterfal.rigor:
The usable quantity is the proton-motive force, the free energy per mole of protons moved across the membrane:

$$\Delta p = \Delta\psi - \frac{2.303\,RT}{F}\,\Delta\mathrm{pH}$$

Two terms, because the gradient stores energy twice: as a voltage $\Delta\psi$ across the membrane and as a concentration difference $\Delta\mathrm{pH}$. The free energy available from moving $n$ moles of protons down it is $\Delta G = -nF\Delta p$, and that is what must exceed the roughly $50\ \mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$ needed to make ATP under cellular conditions.

The turbine is literal, and the gearing is integer. The rotor ring is built from $c$ subunits — between about 8 and 15, depending on the species — and one full turn makes three ATP. So protons per ATP is a ratio of two integers, $c/3$, and it is usually not a whole number: roughly 2.7 in mammals, whose ring has eight, and 4.7 in plant chloroplasts, whose ring has fourteen. The dam has a fixed gear ratio, and evolution chose different gears for different jobs.

recall.question: What does the electron transport chain actually store before any ATP is made?

options.text: A proton gradient across a membrane
options.why: charge on one side and pH difference across it, exactly a reservoir held behind a dam.

options.text: Heat, which is later converted to chemical bonds
options.why: heat is the one form the second law will not let you cash back in at full value.

options.text: ATP itself, released in a burst at the end
options.why: ATP is made by the turbine at the bottom of the fall, not stored in the chain.

options.text: Electrons parked on the final protein
options.why: the electrons end up on oxygen; what persists is the proton imbalance.

bio.cells.membranes-transport.ten-millio.title: Every cell you own holds back a lightning-strength field
bio.cells.membranes-transport.ten-millio.hook: Seventy millivolts across five nanometres is a field several times stronger than the one that turns air into a spark.
bio.cells.membranes-transport.ten-millio.author: author-bio-1

reviewed.notes: The pump does not itself hold the inside negative: named the potassium leak that actually produces the voltage, since "the pump makes the -70 mV" is a standard misconception.

bio.cells.membranes-transport.ten-millio.body:
Take the voltage across a resting cell membrane, about seventy thousandths of a volt, and divide by the thickness of that membrane, about five nanometres. The answer is roughly ten million volts per metre. Dry air breaks down into a spark at around three million. Every cell in your body sits inside a field several times stronger than that, and has done since you were an embryo.

Nothing sparks, because the membrane is a two-molecule-thick sheet of oil, and oil insulates beautifully. A protein called the sodium–potassium pump burns one ATP to throw three sodium ions out and haul two potassium ions in, over and over. The voltage itself appears when potassium leaks back down the gradient the pump built, leaving the inside negative.

That is a charged battery, and a cell spends it like one: to drag glucose uphill against its own concentration, to push waste out, and, in nerve and muscle, to fire. The bill is enormous. A large share of the energy you burn doing nothing at all goes to pumps maintaining a difference across a film you will never see.

recall.question: Why is a resting cell membrane better described as a charged battery than as a wall?
recall.answer: Because pumps burn ATP to hold unequal ion concentrations across it, which stores a voltage. The cell then spends that voltage to move molecules uphill and, in nerve and muscle, to fire.

bio.cells.mitochondria-endosymbiosis.fif.title: The paper that fifteen journals did not want
bio.cells.mitochondria-endosymbiosis.fif.hook: About fifteen journals turned the paper down. It said the powerhouses inside your cells used to be free-living bacteria.
bio.cells.mitochondria-endosymbiosis.fif.author: author-bio-1
bio.cells.mitochondria-endosymbiosis.fif.body:
By her own account it was rejected by about fifteen journals before the *Journal of Theoretical Biology* ran it in 1967. The author, publishing then as Lynn Sagan, claimed that the organelles burning sugar inside every one of your cells are descendants of bacteria that got swallowed and never digested.

Her evidence was circumstantial and strange. Mitochondria carry their own DNA, in a loop, the way bacteria do. They build their own ribosomes, and those ribosomes are bacterial enough that certain antibiotics attack them. They divide by pinching in half on their own schedule; your cell cannot assemble one from parts. They sit inside two membranes, as though the outer one were the leftover wrapping of a meal.

Biologists disliked it, partly because it sounded like a fable about cooperation in a field organised around competition. Then gene sequencing arrived, and mitochondrial genes landed squarely inside one bacterial group, the alphaproteobacteria. You are not one organism that acquired a battery. You are a merger that held.

recall.question: Which observation is the strongest evidence that mitochondria descend from bacteria?

options.text: Their genes place them inside a specific bacterial group on the tree of life
options.why: sequence data puts them among the alphaproteobacteria, which mere resemblance could never do.

options.text: They are shaped like bacteria
options.why: shape is a weak clue; plenty of unrelated structures are sausage-shaped.

options.text: They release energy, and bacteria release energy too
options.why: almost everything alive does, so this separates nothing.

options.text: They appear in every animal cell
options.why: being universal would be just as expected if they had evolved from scratch inside cells.

sources.title: On the Origin of Mitosing Cells, Journal of Theoretical Biology 14(3)
sources.author: Lynn Sagan

bio.cells.signaling.bacteria-take-a-vote.title: Bacteria count themselves, and they refuse to glow until the vote passes
bio.cells.signaling.bacteria-take-a-vote.hook: A single bacterium never glows. Put ten billion of them in a squid's light organ and they all switch on at once.
bio.cells.signaling.bacteria-take-a-vote.author: author-bio-1

reviewed.notes: Repaired a broken sentence in the rigor layer ("fall out that matching the intuition demands").

bio.cells.signaling.bacteria-take-a-vote.body:
A Hawaiian bobtail squid hunts on moonlit nights, and a moonlit squid casts a shadow that something below can see. So it carries a light organ stuffed with the bacterium *Aliivibrio fischeri*, which glows downward and erases the shadow. The squid feeds them; every dawn it vents most of them into the sea.

Here is the part worth stealing. Those same bacteria, floating alone in the ocean, are dark. Making light is expensive and one cell's glow is useless. So each cell leaks a small molecule and listens for it. Diluted in open water the signal drifts away. Packed into the squid's organ at enormous density, the molecule builds up, crosses a threshold, binds its receptor, and the light genes come on — in everybody, nearly at once.

Nealson, Platt and Hastings noticed the effect in 1970 and described it as the cells "conditioning" their medium. It is a collective-action problem solved with a cheap, honest headcount: contribute only when enough others will.
bio.cells.signaling.bacteria-take-a-vote.rigor:
Call $A$ the concentration of the signal molecule. Each cell makes it at a low basal rate, but the signal also switches on its own synthase, so production is autocatalytic. With $n$ cells per unit volume, dilution rate $\gamma$ and a Hill response of order $h$:

$$\frac{dA}{dt} = n\left(a + b\,\frac{A^{h}}{K^{h}+A^{h}}\right) - \gamma A$$

For small $n$ the only intersection of production and removal is a low fixed point: dark. As $n$ grows, the S-shaped production curve lifts until it crosses the line $\gamma A$ in three places, and the system becomes bistable; grow a little further and the low state vanishes entirely, so the cell jumps to the bright branch. That jump is the "vote passing", and it is a saddle-node bifurcation in $n$.

Two features fall out, and they are exactly the ones the intuition demanded: the switch is sharp rather than gradual (the Hill term with $h>1$), and it is hysteretic — having switched on, a population stays lit below the density that lit it.

recall.question: Why does a quorum-sensing population switch on sharply rather than glowing a little more as it grows?

options.text: The signal induces its own production, so the response curve is S-shaped and the low state disappears past a critical density
options.why: a bifurcation, not a dimmer.

options.text: Each cell measures the total population directly and votes
options.why: no cell counts anything; each one only reads a local concentration.

options.text: Light production is all-or-nothing in a single cell
options.why: individual cells can express the genes at intermediate levels; the sharpness comes from the feedback loop.

bio.ecology.biodiversity.ochenta-mil-esp.title: 80.346 especies, y el número se mueve cuando cambia quien cuenta
bio.ecology.biodiversity.ochenta-mil-esp.hook: 80.346 especies registradas al cierre de 2024. La cifra dice tanto sobre la biología del país como sobre quién se puso a contar.
bio.ecology.biodiversity.ochenta-mil-esp.author: author-bio-1

reviewed.notes: Cut unverified counts (1,966 birds; 8,500 endemics) and the "cierra cada 31 de diciembre" framing. Kept SiB's verified December-2024 figures and added the 4th-place methodology point, which is the card's thesis.

bio.ecology.biodiversity.ochenta-mil-esp.body:
El SiB Colombia hace corte a diciembre. Al cierre de 2024 el país llevaba 80.346 especies registradas: primero del mundo en aves, en orquídeas y en mariposas; segundo en anfibios, peces de agua dulce, palmas y murciélagos; tercero en plantas. Unas 4.270 especies de orquídeas, más de 9.000 endémicas y 2.104 con algún grado de amenaza —466 en peligro crítico, 800 en peligro, 838 vulnerables—.

Vale la pena leer bien qué es ese número. No es un censo de lo que existe: es un registro de lo que alguien documentó, publicó y subió a una base de datos. Sube cada año en parte porque aparecen especies nuevas y en parte porque hay más gente colectando, digitalizando colecciones viejas y corrigiendo nombres.

Y con esa misma cifra Colombia pasó al cuarto puesto mundial, detrás de Brasil, Indonesia y China. El propio SiB aclara que el descenso viene de ajustes metodológicos, no de biodiversidad perdida. Ahí está el punto entero: la cifra mide la naturaleza y mide la infraestructura que la mira.

recall.question: ¿Por qué el número de especies registradas en Colombia sube todos los años?

options.text: Porque es un registro acumulado de lo documentado, y crece tanto por especies nuevas como por colecciones que apenas se están digitalizando
options.why: mide biología y capacidad de observación a la vez.

options.text: Porque la biodiversidad del país está aumentando
options.why: la pérdida de hábitat empuja en la dirección contraria; lo que crece es el conocimiento.

options.text: Porque se cuentan también las especies introducidas
options.why: el registro incluye introducidas, pero no explican el crecimiento sostenido.

options.text: Porque cambia la definición de especie cada año
options.why: los cambios taxonómicos ocurren, y a veces restan; no son el motor de la curva.

sources.title: Lista oficial de aves de Colombia (Asociación Colombiana de Ornitología)

bio.ecology.biogeography.el-dibujo-del-c.title: El dibujo que bajó del Chimborazo
bio.ecology.biogeography.el-dibujo-del-c.hook: Humboldt subió el Chimborazo en 1802 y bajó con un dibujo. Ese dibujo fundó la biogeografía.
bio.ecology.biogeography.el-dibujo-del-c.author: author-bio-1
bio.ecology.biogeography.el-dibujo-del-c.body:
En 1801 Alexander von Humboldt llegó a Bogotá con una obsesión y una carta de presentación. Venía a conocer a José Celestino Mutis, director de la Real Expedición Botánica, y lo recibieron casi como a un jefe de Estado: sesenta jinetes y el coche del arzobispo.

El 23 de junio de 1802, ya en los Andes ecuatorianos, subió el Chimborazo con Bonpland y Carlos Montúfar hasta unos 5.875 metros —su propio barómetro le daba algo más— y no llegó a la cumbre: una grieta, el soroche, las encías sangrando. Fue, durante décadas, la mayor altura registrada por un europeo.

Lo que se trajo no fue el récord. Fue un corte transversal de la montaña con las plantas ordenadas por altura: el *Tableau physique*. En una sola lámina se ve la tesis: subir mil metros hace lo mismo que caminar cientos de kilómetros hacia el polo. La vida no se reparte por capricho sino por temperatura, presión y humedad.

Eso es biogeografía, y empezó como un dibujo.

recall.question: ¿Cuál es la idea que el *Tableau physique* del Chimborazo puso por primera vez en una sola imagen?
recall.answer: Que la distribución de los seres vivos es función de variables físicas: la altitud reproduce lo que hace la latitud. Subir por una montaña tropical equivale a viajar hacia las zonas frías, y los pisos de vegetación se ordenan por temperatura y presión, no por región.

bio.ecology.climate-and-life.bogota-bebe.title: Bogotá bebe de una planta peluda
bio.ecology.climate-and-life.bogota-bebe.hook: Colombia tiene cerca de la mitad de los páramos del mundo, y 17 millones de personas toman agua que pasó primero por hojas peludas.
bio.ecology.climate-and-life.bogota-bebe.author: author-bio-1

reviewed.notes: Removed the unsourced "16 ciudades" and an unverifiable frailejon growth range; kept the verified Humboldt Institute figures (2.9 Mha, 36 complejos, 2.5%, 17 million people).

bio.ecology.climate-and-life.bogota-bebe.body:
El páramo solo existe en el norte de los Andes, entre el bosque y la nieve, y Colombia alberga cerca de la mitad del que hay en el mundo: más de 2,9 millones de hectáreas repartidas en 36 complejos, sobre apenas el 2,5% del territorio continental. De ahí sale el agua de unos 17 millones de personas, Bogotá incluida.

El truco físico lo hace el frailejón. Sus hojas son gruesas y están cubiertas de pelos blancos que peinan la niebla: el vapor se condensa en ellas, el agua escurre por el tallo esponjoso y se entrega despacio al suelo. El páramo no almacena lluvia tanto como *captura nube*, y luego la suelta a lo largo del año en lugar de mandarla toda río abajo en un aguacero.

Crece a paso de geología. Se repite mucho que un centímetro al año; sirve como orden de magnitud, no como reloj, porque las tasas medidas cambian bastante entre especies y entre altitudes. Aun así la cuenta asusta: un frailejón de dos metros lleva ahí un par de siglos, peinando neblina desde antes de que Bogotá tuviera acueducto.

recall.question: ¿Por qué se dice que el páramo es infraestructura de agua y no solo un paisaje?

options.text: Regula: capta agua de la niebla y la entrega al suelo poco a poco, de modo que los ríos bajan con caudal en época seca
options.why: es un embalse con vegetación.

options.text: Porque allí llueve más que en cualquier otro ecosistema del país
options.why: la Amazonía y el Pacífico reciben mucha más lluvia; lo del páramo es la regulación, no el volumen.

options.text: Porque los frailejones producen agua químicamente
options.why: la condensan de la niebla; no la fabrican.

options.text: Porque está por encima de las ciudades y el agua baja sola
options.why: la gravedad ayuda, pero sin la esponja de suelo y planta el agua bajaría de golpe y faltaría en verano.

bio.ecology.ecosystems-energy.how-much-g.title: How much grass is a lion?
bio.ecology.ecosystems-energy.how-much-g.hook: Work out why nothing on land eats lions, using one number and two multiplications.
bio.ecology.ecosystems-energy.how-much-g.author: author-bio-1
bio.ecology.ecosystems-energy.how-much-g.body:
Energy climbs a food chain badly. Almost everything an antelope eats is spent staying warm, moving, and being an antelope; only a small fraction ends up as antelope that a lion could eat.

So: to add one kilogram of new lion to the savannah, roughly how many kilograms of plants have to be grown? Work it out with a single efficiency figure applied twice.

Then the question the arithmetic answers for free: why is there no land animal that makes its living by eating lions?

recall.question: The number, and why food chains are short.
recall.answer: The rule of thumb is that about 10% of the energy at one level becomes biomass at the next — Lindeman's 1942 figure, though he never called it a law and reported efficiencies anywhere from 0.1% to 37.5%. Grass → antelope → lion is two steps, so roughly 100 kg of plants per kilogram of lion; a lion-eater would need about 1,000. Each step divides the available energy by ten, so by the fourth or fifth level there is not enough left to feed a viable population. That is also why top predators are rare and need enormous territories.

sources.title: The Trophic-Dynamic Aspect of Ecology, Ecology 23(4), 399–417
sources.author: Raymond L. Lindeman

bio.ecology.population-dynamics.lynx-and.title: Remember phase portraits? Lynx and hares drew one
bio.ecology.population-dynamics.lynx-and.hook: A century of fur-trade ledgers, two coupled ODEs, and closed orbits that never settle and never die.
bio.ecology.population-dynamics.lynx-and.author: author-bio-1
bio.ecology.population-dynamics.lynx-and.body:
You learned to read trajectories in the plane: fixed points, nullclines, orbits that close or spiral. Here is the same picture with fur in it.

The Hudson's Bay Company logged pelts for more than a century, and when Elton and Nicholson plotted lynx against snowshoe hare in 1942 the two series rose and fell on a roughly ten-year cycle, the predator trailing the prey. Volterra had already written equations that do that, in 1926, for a different reason: his son-in-law had noticed that the share of predatory fish in Adriatic catches went *up* during the First World War, when the boats stayed in port. Lotka had the same system in 1925.

Be careful with the ledgers. They count pelts traded, not animals alive, and the hare cycle is not a two-species affair — a Yukon field experiment found food and predation together produce an eleven-fold effect, far more than either alone. In the fur data the lynx peak sometimes even appears to *precede* the hare peak, which is almost certainly an artefact of trapping.

What the model does deliver is exact.
bio.ecology.population-dynamics.lynx-and.rigor:
$$\dot{x}=\alpha x-\beta x y, \qquad \dot{y}=-\gamma y+\delta x y .$$

Fixed points: the origin (a saddle) and $(x^{*},y^{*})=(\gamma/\delta,\ \alpha/\beta)$, where the Jacobian has eigenvalues $\pm i\sqrt{\alpha\gamma}$ — purely imaginary, so linearisation is inconclusive. The quantity

$$V=\delta x-\gamma\ln x+\beta y-\alpha\ln y$$

is conserved, so every trajectory lies on a level set of $V$: a genuine centre, closed orbits, no damping. It is also structurally unstable — the smallest realistic perturbation turns the centre into a spiral, which is why nobody claims real populations sit on these curves.

Two exact consequences survive anyway. Divide the first equation by $x$: $\frac{d}{dt}\ln x=\alpha-\beta y$. Integrate over one period and the left side vanishes, giving $\bar{y}=\alpha/\beta$; the same move gives $\bar{x}=\gamma/\delta$. **Time averages equal the fixed point**, whatever loop you are on.

Now harvest both species at rate $h$: $\alpha\mapsto\alpha-h$, $\gamma\mapsto\gamma+h$. The averages become $\bar{y}=(\alpha-h)/\beta$ and $\bar{x}=(\gamma+h)/\delta$. Killing indiscriminately *raises* mean prey and *lowers* mean predators — so stopping fishing does the reverse. That is Volterra's principle, and it is what the Adriatic catch data had been showing all along.

recall.question: The Lotka–Volterra system has a centre, not a stable spiral. Why does that matter for using it on real data?

options.text: The amplitude of the cycle is set entirely by initial conditions and never decays
options.why: and the centre is destroyed by any small perturbation, so real cycles need extra structure to explain.

options.text: It means the populations must eventually go extinct
options.why: orbits are closed and periodic; neither species dies out in the model.

options.text: It means the model has no equilibrium
options.why: it has one, at $(\gamma/\delta,\alpha/\beta)$, and that point is the time average of every orbit.

options.text: It means the predator and prey peak simultaneously
options.why: they cannot; the predator peak lags the prey peak by a quarter cycle.

bio.evolution.coevolution.darwin-orders-.title: Darwin looked at an orchid and ordered a moth
bio.evolution.coevolution.darwin-orders-.hook: A flower with a foot-long nectar tube made Darwin predict an unseen moth. Nobody watched one drink from it for 135 years.
bio.evolution.coevolution.darwin-orders-.author: author-bio-1

reviewed.notes: The 1992 photographs and 2004 video are not documented; the published first record is Wasserthal 1997. Fixed body and hook, added the Wasserthal paper as a source.

bio.evolution.coevolution.darwin-orders-.body:
In January 1862 a box of Madagascan orchids reached Down House. One of them, *Angraecum sesquipedale*, had a green nectar tube nearly a foot long with the nectar only at the very bottom. Darwin wrote to Hooker: "Good Heavens what insect can suck it". Then he did the unfashionable thing and predicted the insect — a moth with a tongue long enough to reach. Wallace went further in 1867, pointing at a likely African relative and saying naturalists should hunt for the Madagascan one with the confidence astronomers had when they went looking for Neptune.

In 1903 Rothschild and Jordan described a Madagascan hawkmoth with a proboscis that long, and gave it the epithet *praedicta*. Nobody published a record of one actually drinking from the flower until Lutz Wasserthal's Madagascan fieldwork, reported in 1997 — 135 years after Darwin asked. In 2021 the moth was raised to a full species, *Xanthopan praedicta*.

The tube and the tongue built each other. Each species is the other's environment, and that environment keeps moving.
bio.evolution.coevolution.darwin-orders-.rigor:
Coevolution changes what "adapted" means: fitness is measured against a landscape that the other player is deforming. Leigh Van Valen turned that into a testable claim in 1973. Plot the fraction of fossil genera in a group still surviving after $t$ million years. If the curve is log-linear,

$$S(t)=e^{-\lambda t},$$

then the hazard rate is constant: $P(\text{extinct in }[t,t+dt]\mid \text{survived to }t)=\lambda\,dt$, independent of $t$. Extinction is memoryless. A lineage that has been winning for fifty million years is in no less danger than a new one.

That is the Red Queen: improvement buys no lasting safety, because everything you interact with is improving too. Van Valen called it a law of constant extinction; how well the log-linearity really holds across taxa has been argued about ever since, and the modern reading keeps the mechanism — adaptation is relative — while treating the constant hazard as an approximation.

The same logic pays rent elsewhere. The leading explanation for why sex is worth its two-fold cost is Red Queen dynamics against parasites: recombination keeps shuffling the lock while the parasites keep filing keys.

recall.question: What does a constant extinction hazard imply about being well adapted?

options.text: Past success buys no future safety
options.why: the risk of extinction is memoryless, because competitors and parasites improve as fast as you do.

options.text: Species get more robust as they age
options.why: that is what a *falling* hazard would mean, and it is what the fossil curves do not show.

options.text: Extinction is caused mainly by external catastrophes
options.why: mass extinctions are real, but a constant background hazard points at ongoing biotic pressure.

options.text: Adaptation does not happen
options.why: it happens constantly; it just does not accumulate into a permanent advantage.

sources.title: The Pollinators of the Malagasy Star Orchids Angraecum sesquipedale, A. sororium and A. compactum, Botanica Acta 110(5), 343–359
sources.author: Lutz T. Wasserthal

bio.evolution.darwin-wallace.the-letter-.title: The envelope that ended twenty years of not publishing
bio.evolution.darwin-wallace.the-letter-.hook: Darwin sat on the idea for twenty years. It took one envelope from a Malay island to get him to publish.
bio.evolution.darwin-wallace.the-letter-.author: author-bio-1
bio.evolution.darwin-wallace.the-letter-.body:
Darwin had the argument by 1838 and a 230-page essay by 1844, with written instructions telling his wife how to publish it if he died. Then he left it in a drawer for fourteen years and wrote about barnacles instead.

On 18 June 1858 a package arrived from the Malay Archipelago. Alfred Russel Wallace, a collector fourteen years younger who funded himself by selling specimens, had worked out the same mechanism during a fever on Ternate that February and posted it to the one famous naturalist he thought might pass it along. Darwin wrote to Lyell that day: he had been forestalled.

The compromise was a joint reading at the Linnean Society on 1 July 1858. Neither man was in the room. Wallace was still in the archipelago; Darwin was burying his infant son, dead of scarlet fever three days before. Nobody reacted. The society's president, Thomas Bell, wrote in his address the next year that 1858 "has not, indeed, been marked by any of those striking discoveries which at once revolutionize" a field.

*On the Origin of Species* went on sale sixteen months later.

recall.question: What actually forced Darwin to publish in 1858?

options.text: Wallace independently derived natural selection and mailed it to him, creating a priority problem overnight
options.why: twenty years of caution ended in a fortnight.

options.text: New fossil evidence finally settled the question
options.why: the fossil record was one of Darwin's own listed difficulties, not his trigger.

options.text: The Linnean Society commissioned the paper from him
options.why: the Society hosted a hasty joint reading arranged by his friends to share credit.

options.text: He finished the long book he had been writing
options.why: the *Origin* was written afterwards, as an "abstract" of the book he never completed.

sources.title: On the Tendency of Species to form Varieties (the Darwin–Wallace papers, 1858)

bio.evolution.drift-neutral.nobodys-faul.title: Most of evolution is nobody's fault
bio.evolution.drift-neutral.nobodys-faul.hook: Two lines of algebra in which the population size cancels out — and a clock appears with nothing ticking.
bio.evolution.drift-neutral.nobodys-faul.author: author-bio-1
bio.evolution.drift-neutral.nobodys-faul.body:
Hardy–Weinberg says nothing moves unless something pushes. There are two pushes. One has a direction: selection. The other is pure sampling noise. In a finite population, the alleles that make it into the next generation are a random draw, and random draws wander. In a population of a thousand, a variant can go from rare to universal on luck alone.

In 1968 Motoo Kimura argued that at the molecular level luck does most of the work. His evidence was a rate. Proteins were turning out to accumulate changes at a roughly constant pace per year, similar across lineages with wildly different lives, and the total pace looked too fast for selection to be paying for every one of them.

Then he gave an argument that was very hard to dismiss: two lines of arithmetic in which the population size cancels out.
bio.evolution.drift-neutral.nobodys-faul.rigor:
Let $\mu$ be the rate of *neutral* mutation per gamete per generation, and let the population hold $2N$ copies of each gene.

New neutral mutants arising per generation: $2N\mu$. Probability that any one of them eventually takes over: under drift alone a neutral allele fixes with probability equal to its current frequency, and a brand-new mutant sits at $1/(2N)$. So the substitution rate is

$$k \;=\; 2N\mu \cdot \frac{1}{2N} \;=\; \mu .$$

The population size vanishes. Differences between two lineages accumulate at the neutral mutation rate no matter how large or small either population has been. That cancellation *is* the molecular clock: a clock with nothing ticking.

Drift's other signature is its noise. The change in allele frequency $p$ over one generation has variance $p(1-p)/(2N)$, so heterozygosity decays by a factor $\left(1-\tfrac{1}{2N}\right)$ each generation. Selection is audible above that noise only when $|s|\gtrsim 1/(2N)$ — the drift barrier. In a small population, a mildly beneficial mutation is indistinguishable from luck.

Kimura never claimed selection was unimportant, or that beaks and eyes are accidents. He claimed most *substitutions* are invisible to selection, which makes neutrality the null model you must reject before announcing adaptation.

Selection. Drift. Transmission. Three separate accounts. Is there one line that holds all of them at once?

recall.question: Why does the neutral substitution rate not depend on population size?

options.text: A big population makes proportionally more mutants ($2N\mu$) but each one is proportionally less likely to fix ($1/2N$)
options.why: the two factors cancel exactly.

options.text: Because large populations have lower mutation rates per individual
options.why: mutation rates per gamete are not set by population size.

options.text: Because drift is negligible in large populations, so only mutation matters
options.why: drift is weaker in large populations, but the fixation probability falls at exactly the same rate.

options.text: Because natural selection compensates for the difference
options.why: the calculation assumes no selection at all; that is what "neutral" means.

sources.title: Evolutionary rate at the molecular level, Nature 217, 624–626
sources.author: Motoo Kimura

bio.evolution.evo-devo.a-mouse-gene-buil.title: A mouse gene, dropped into a fly, orders an eye
bio.evolution.evo-devo.a-mouse-gene-buil.hook: Switch a fly gene on in the wrong place and the fly grows an eye there. Switch on the mouse version and it works just as well.
bio.evolution.evo-devo.a-mouse-gene-buil.author: author-bio-1
bio.evolution.evo-devo.a-mouse-gene-buil.body:
In 1995 Walter Gehring's lab in Basel forced a fly gene called *eyeless* to switch on in tissue that was supposed to become a leg, or a wing, or an antenna. The flies grew eyes there: structured, pigmented compound eyes, in the wrong places.

Then the result that still sounds made up. The mouse version of that gene, *Pax6*, does the same job in a fly. A gene from a mammal, expressed in a fly's leg, triggers the construction of a *fly's* compound eye — not a mouse eye, not a hybrid. The instruction and the machinery it calls are separable, and the instruction is old enough to be shared by animals whose last common ancestor may not have had eyes worth the name.

That separation is the whole thesis of evolutionary developmental biology: big changes in form often come from switching ancient genes on at new times and places, not from inventing new genes.
bio.evolution.evo-devo.a-mouse-gene-buil.rigor:
*Pax6* encodes a transcription factor with two DNA-binding domains, a paired domain and a homeodomain. It sits near the top of a regulatory network — *eyes absent*, *sine oculis*, *dachshund* and others — with feedback among the members. Calling it "the master control gene for the eye" is a simplification Gehring himself argued about: it is sufficient to launch the cascade in competent tissue, which is not the same as being the thing that specifies an eye.

The precise claim is **deep homology**. Fly and vertebrate eyes are not homologous as organs; they are built from different tissues on different plans. What is homologous is the genetic switch that initiates them. Conservation lives in the circuit, not in the product.

The same pattern shows up at body scale in the *Hox* genes, a cluster of transcription factors with a property that has no obvious reason to be true: they are arranged along the chromosome in the same order as the body regions they specify, head to tail. That spatial colinearity holds in flies and in us, which is why an ordering on a piece of DNA is also a map of an animal.

recall.question: A mouse *Pax6* gene expressed in a fly's leg produces a fly's compound eye, not a mouse eye. What does that show?

options.text: The trigger is conserved while the machinery it calls is local
options.why: deep homology of the switch, not of the organ.

options.text: Fly and mouse eyes are the same organ inherited from a common ancestor
options.why: they differ in tissue and plan; only the initiating circuit is shared.

options.text: *Pax6* contains the blueprint for an eye
options.why: it is a transcription factor; the blueprint is the network of genes it turns on in that tissue.

options.text: Mice and flies are more closely related than anyone thought
options.why: the relationship is ancient; what is surprising is how little the switch has changed.

sources.title: Induction of Ectopic Eyes by Targeted Expression of the eyeless Gene in Drosophila, Science 267, 1788–1792
sources.author: Georg Halder, Patrick Callaerts, Walter J. Gehring

bio.evolution.evolutionary-games.nash-wi.title: Remember Nash equilibrium? Evolution found a stricter version
bio.evolution.evolutionary-games.nash-wi.hook: Nash assumed players who reason. Evolution has none, gets equilibrium anyway, and its version is strictly stronger.
bio.evolution.evolutionary-games.nash-wi.author: author-bio-1

reviewed.notes: Fixed callback.from (was econ.game-theory.evolutionary, which gates the card behind the idea it teaches) to dominance-nash; corrected "Nash equilibria are exactly the rest points" — the converse fails.

bio.evolution.evolutionary-games.nash-wi.body:
When you met Nash equilibrium, the justification was psychological: rational players, common knowledge, nobody wants to deviate given what everyone else does. In 1973 Maynard Smith and Price asked what survives if you delete the players. No reasoning, no beliefs, no common knowledge. Strategies are inherited, payoff is offspring, and the population plays against itself.

Equilibrium survives, and it comes back sharper. A strategy is *evolutionarily stable* if a population playing it cannot be invaded: any rare mutant does strictly worse than the residents do, so selection removes it. That is not a new solution concept bolted onto Nash. It is Nash plus one extra requirement, and the extra requirement bites.

Their example is Hawk–Dove. Two animals contest a resource worth $V$; a fight costs $C$. Doves share, hawks escalate, and when two hawks meet they split the spoils and the injuries. If $C>V$, neither pure strategy is stable — a population of doves is invaded by hawks, a population of hawks by doves — and the stable mixture is exactly $V/C$ hawks.

The relationship to Nash is a containment, and it is strict.
bio.evolution.evolutionary-games.nash-wi.rigor:
A strategy $S$ is an **ESS** if, for every $T \neq S$, either

$$E(S,S) > E(T,S), \qquad\text{or}\qquad E(S,S) = E(T,S)\ \text{ and }\ E(S,T) > E(T,T).$$

The first clause says $S$ is a strict best reply to itself; the second handles ties by asking that $S$ do better against the invader than the invader does against itself. Condition one alone is strict Nash, so **every ESS is a Nash equilibrium of the symmetric game, and the inclusion is proper**: rock–paper–scissors has a unique Nash equilibrium (uniform) which is not an ESS, because every alternative ties against it and does no worse against itself.

Hawk–Dove, checked. With hawk frequency $p$,

$$E(H)=p\frac{V-C}{2}+(1-p)V,\qquad E(D)=(1-p)\frac{V}{2},$$

and equating them gives $p^{*}=V/C$ for $V<C$.

The dynamic version replaces "cannot be invaded" with an ODE. Under the replicator equation $\dot{x}_i = x_i\left(f_i(x)-\bar{f}(x)\right)$, every Nash equilibrium is a rest point. The converse fails — every pure state is a rest point, however bad — but the good direction is enough: every ESS is an asymptotically stable rest point. Equilibrium without a single reasoning agent: the fixed point of a differential equation, reached by dying.

recall.question: What does an ESS require that a Nash equilibrium does not?

options.text: That rare mutants be actively driven out
options.why: if a mutant ties against the incumbent, the incumbent must still beat it in mutant-versus-mutant play.

options.text: That the strategy be pure rather than mixed
options.why: the Hawk–Dove ESS is a mixture, $V/C$ hawks.

options.text: That players know each other's payoffs
options.why: evolutionary games work precisely because nobody knows anything.

options.text: That the game be zero-sum
options.why: nothing in the definition constrains the payoff structure that way.

sources.title: The logic of animal conflict, Nature 246, 15–18
sources.author: John Maynard Smith and George R. Price

bio.evolution.human-evolution.still-in-y.title: A species that vanished 40,000 years ago is still inside you
bio.evolution.human-evolution.still-in-y.hook: Neanderthals disappeared around 40,000 years ago. If your ancestry runs outside Africa, roughly 2% of you is theirs.
bio.evolution.human-evolution.still-in-y.author: author-bio-1
bio.evolution.human-evolution.still-in-y.body: Svante Pääbo's group published a draft Neanderthal genome in 2010, read from bone powder. People with ancestry outside Africa carry a small Neanderthal fraction — the first estimate was one to four per cent, and current figures cluster near two. It is not inert filler: some of those inherited variants affect immunity and skin. Pääbo took the 2022 Nobel for making dead DNA readable at all.

recall.question: What does a couple of per cent of Neanderthal DNA in living people actually demonstrate?
recall.answer: That the two populations interbred, and that some of the resulting variants were kept. Interbreeding happened; the descendants are us.

sources.author: Richard E. Green et al.

bio.evolution.kin-selection-altruism.dyi.title: The arithmetic of dying for your brother
bio.evolution.kin-selection-altruism.dyi.hook: Two brothers, or eight cousins. The arithmetic is real; the pub quote it is famous for probably is not.
bio.evolution.kin-selection-altruism.dyi.author: author-bio-1
bio.evolution.kin-selection-altruism.dyi.body:
J. B. S. Haldane did the sum in print in 1955: a gene that makes you sacrifice yourself can still spread, provided the sacrifice saves more than two brothers, or four half-brothers, or eight first cousins. That is the real, citable version.

The famous version — Haldane in a pub, on the back of an envelope, announcing he would lay down his life for two brothers or eight cousins — reaches us second-hand. John Maynard Smith published the anecdote in 1975; Hamilton himself said he was dismayed by it and doubted the phrasing. Treat the scene as a story and the numbers as arithmetic.

The arithmetic is Hamilton's, from 1964. Copies of a gene do not care which body they sit in. So a behaviour that costs the actor and benefits a relative can pay, if the relative is likely enough to be carrying the same copy. Sterile worker bees, alarm calls that draw the hawk, birds that skip breeding to feed a sibling's chicks — all of them stop being paradoxes and become accounting.

Here is the inequality that does the accounting.
bio.evolution.kin-selection-altruism.dyi.rigor:
**Hamilton's rule.** A social act is favoured when

$$r\,b \;>\; c,$$

with $c$ the fitness cost to the actor, $b$ the fitness benefit to the recipient, and $r$ their relatedness. Hamilton's own 1964 statement was $K > 1/r$ for $K=b/c$; the $rb>c$ form is a later standardisation of the same inequality.

$r$ is not "fraction of DNA shared" — you share about 99.9% of your genome with any human. It is a regression coefficient: how much better than the population baseline the recipient predicts the actor's genotype. Full siblings $r=\tfrac12$, half-siblings $\tfrac14$, first cousins $\tfrac18$. So Haldane's numbers are break-even points: $2\times\tfrac12 = 1$ and $8\times\tfrac18 = 1$.

Inclusive fitness is then the actor's own reproduction plus the sum of $r_j b_j$ over everyone it helps. Where it breaks: the rule as stated assumes costs and benefits add, and that $r$ is measured against the right baseline. The old star argument — that haplodiploid Hymenoptera evolve sterile castes because sisters share $r=\tfrac34$ — has not held up on its own, since termites are diplodiploid and eusocial; lifetime monogamy of the queen turns out to matter more.

recall.question: In Hamilton's rule, what does the relatedness coefficient $r$ actually measure?

options.text: How much more likely than a random population member the recipient is to carry the actor's allele
options.why: a regression, not a raw percentage of shared DNA.

options.text: The fraction of the genome two individuals share
options.why: by that measure any two humans are over 99% related and the rule would predict universal altruism.

options.text: The probability that two individuals were born to the same mother
options.why: that is one special case; the rule covers cousins, nieces and clones alike.

options.text: How similar two individuals look
options.why: resemblance is a noisy proxy that selection cannot compute directly.

sources.title: The Genetical Evolution of Social Behaviour, I, Journal of Theoretical Biology 7(1), 1–16
sources.author: W. D. Hamilton

sources.title: Two Brothers or Eight Cousins (provenance of the Haldane quip)

bio.evolution.natural-selection.selectio.title: Remember Darwin's three facts? That is a definition of learning
bio.evolution.natural-selection.selectio.hook: Variation, heredity, differential success. Rename the three and you have written down what 'learning' means in machine learning.
bio.evolution.natural-selection.selectio.author: author-bio-1
bio.evolution.natural-selection.selectio.body:
Variation, heredity, differential success. You met those as an argument about finches. They are also, word for word, the specification of an optimisation procedure, and the machine-learning version renames rather than rebuilds them.

Mutation and recombination become proposals for new parameters. Fitness becomes the negative of a loss. A generation becomes a training step. The population becomes the set of candidates currently in play. Both procedures keep what scores well and discard the rest; neither needs a designer, a written-down goal, or any understanding of *why* the winner won. That is the whole reason a textbook can define learning as "performance on a task improves with experience" without saying who is doing the improving.

Now the difference, which is the entire practical story. Gradient descent knows which direction to move, because it differentiates the loss. Evolution cannot differentiate anything. It can only evaluate. That makes selection a zeroth-order method, and zeroth-order methods pay for their generality.
bio.evolution.natural-selection.selectio.rigor:
Take the discrete replicator update on a population of types with frequencies $x_i$ and fitnesses $f_i$:

$$x_i' \;=\; \frac{x_i f_i}{\sum_j x_j f_j}.$$

That is Bayes' rule. Read $x_i$ as a prior over hypotheses, $f_i$ as the likelihood of the observed data under hypothesis $i$, and $x_i'$ as the posterior. A population's frequency vector and a Bayesian's belief vector obey the same recursion; Harper (2009) develops the correspondence through information geometry. Selection is inference, with dying as the update rule.

The cost of having no gradient is also exact. Evolution strategies estimate the gradient of a smoothed objective by sampling:

$$\nabla_\theta\,\mathbb{E}_{\varepsilon\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I)}\big[f(\theta+\sigma\varepsilon)\big] \;=\; \frac{1}{\sigma}\,\mathbb{E}_{\varepsilon}\big[f(\theta+\sigma\varepsilon)\,\varepsilon\big].$$

Every evaluation contributes one scalar, so the estimator's variance grows with dimension, whereas backpropagation returns all $d$ partial derivatives for roughly the cost of one forward pass. Salimans et al. (2017) showed the trade is worth making when you have thousands of machines and no gradient — which is exactly evolution's situation, run for four billion years on a very large cluster.

recall.question: What is the sharpest difference between natural selection and gradient descent?

options.text: Selection only evaluates candidates, while gradient descent differentiates the objective and so knows which direction to move
options.why: one scalar per trial versus a full gradient.

options.text: Selection has no objective function, while learning does
options.why: fitness is an objective function; nobody has to write it down for it to act as one.

options.text: Selection is random and gradient descent is deterministic
options.why: mutation is random, but stochastic gradient descent is too; the difference is the derivative.

options.text: Selection works on populations, learning on a single model
options.why: population methods are standard in optimisation, and evolution strategies use them deliberately.

bio.evolution.natural-selection.three-fa.title: Three facts and one conclusion
bio.evolution.natural-selection.three-fa.hook: Darwin's argument mentions no genes, no DNA, not even life. It is three observations and a conclusion that cannot be refused.
bio.evolution.natural-selection.three-fa.author: author-bio-1
bio.evolution.natural-selection.three-fa.body:
In September 1838 Darwin read Malthus on population growth, and the argument closed. It has three premises.

More individuals are born than can possibly survive. Individuals differ from one another. Some of those differences pass to offspring.

The conclusion follows without any further biology: individuals whose differences happen to help them survive and reproduce leave more offspring, and those offspring tend to carry the same differences. Run it again. Nothing in that chain mentions genes, cells, or even life — which is why the same argument turns up in economics, in immunology, and in every optimisation algorithm that keeps what works and discards what does not.

That generality is the point. Darwin was not proposing a force. He was pointing at an accounting identity that any system with copying, variation and unequal success cannot escape.

Which raises the awkward part. Premise three says traits are inherited. Darwin had no theory of how. And the theory of heredity most Victorians actually believed would have destroyed his argument in about ten generations.
bio.evolution.natural-selection.three-fa.rigor:
Lewontin (1970) put the premises in their minimal form. Evolution by natural selection occurs in any population with:

1. **Variation** — individuals differ in some trait $z$.
2. **Differential fitness** — the expected number of offspring $w$ depends on $z$.
3. **Heritability** — offspring resemble their parents in $z$.

All three are necessary. Drop variation and there is nothing to select. Drop the fitness–trait relationship and the changes are random. Drop heritability and every generation starts from scratch: selection still happens, it just leaves no trace.

Notice what is *not* on the list. No mention of DNA, sexual reproduction, species, or organisms. The conditions are satisfied by molecules in a test tube, by firms in a market, by antibodies in your lymph nodes. This is why biologists say natural selection is substrate-neutral, and why "survival of the fittest" is a bad summary: fitness here just means expected reproductive output, so the phrase says nothing that the three conditions do not already say.

Episode 5 turns these three sentences into one equation. First, heredity.

recall.question: Which of Darwin's three conditions is the one he could not explain in 1859?

options.text: Heredity
options.why: he had no mechanism for how offspring resemble parents, and the going theory of inheritance actively undermined him.

options.text: Variation
options.why: that individuals differ was the least controversial thing in the book; breeders had known it for centuries.

options.text: Overproduction
options.why: Malthus had already made the case, and Darwin took the premise directly from him.

sources.title: The Units of Selection, Annual Review of Ecology and Systematics 1
sources.author: Richard C. Lewontin

bio.evolution.phylogenetics.a-third-kind.title: He found a third kind of life by reading one molecule
bio.evolution.phylogenetics.a-third-kind.hook: In 1977 one molecule revealed a whole domain of life that nobody had noticed, and the field's reaction was to tell him to stop.
bio.evolution.phylogenetics.a-third-kind.author: author-bio-1

reviewed.notes: Added sources for the Luria and Mayr objections, which no cited source carried (three-domain system; Mayr 1998 PNAS).

bio.evolution.phylogenetics.a-third-kind.body:
Until 1977 the living world came in two boxes: cells with a nucleus and cells without. Carl Woese ignored anatomy altogether. He picked a single molecule that every organism on Earth has — the small subunit of ribosomal RNA, part of the machine that turns genes into proteins — and compared its sequence across species, betting that something this essential changes slowly and honestly.

What came out was a set of "bacteria" from hot springs and cow stomachs that were not bacteria. Their ribosomal RNA sat about as far from bacteria as it did from us. Woese and George Fox announced three primary lines of descent where everyone had seen two.

The reception was rough. Salvador Luria told a colleague to dissociate himself from the nonsense, and Ernst Mayr never accepted it. Some of the anger was about manners: the claim went out by press release and reached the front page of the *New York Times* on 3 November 1977. Within a decade it was textbook.
bio.evolution.phylogenetics.a-third-kind.rigor:
A phylogeny is a tree whose leaves are the taxa and whose internal nodes are inferred ancestors. The trouble is the search space. The number of unrooted binary trees on $n$ labelled leaves is the double factorial

$$(2n-5)!! \;=\; 1\cdot 3\cdot 5\cdots(2n-5),$$

which for a modest $n=20$ is about $2.2\times 10^{20}$. Nobody enumerates. You optimise instead: parsimony picks the tree needing fewest character changes, distance methods cluster on pairwise divergence, and likelihood or Bayesian methods score trees under an explicit model of how sequences mutate.

The model is not decoration. The classic failure is **long-branch attraction**: two lineages evolving quickly will land on the same base at the same site by coincidence — with only four possible letters, coincidences are cheap — and parsimony reads the coincidence as shared ancestry, pulling unrelated fast branches together. Model-based methods are less vulnerable, not immune.

Woese's real design decision was the molecule. Ribosomal RNA is universal, functionally constrained enough to stay alignable across domains, and rarely swapped between unrelated organisms — the three properties that make a molecular character a usable clock rather than a rumour.

recall.question: Why did Woese compare ribosomal RNA rather than, say, a metabolic gene?

options.text: It is present in every organism, changes slowly because its function is tightly constrained, and is rarely transferred between lineages
options.why: so it stays comparable across the deepest splits.

options.text: It is the longest molecule in the cell, giving the most data
options.why: length is not the constraint; alignability across billions of years is.

options.text: It mutates fastest, so differences accumulate quickly
options.why: fast mutation destroys deep signal and invites long-branch attraction.

options.text: It was the only sequence available in 1977
options.why: several proteins had been sequenced; the choice was deliberate, not forced.

bio.evolution.sexual-selection.the-feath.title: The feather that made Darwin sick
bio.evolution.sexual-selection.the-feath.hook: A peacock's tail is a survival disaster. Darwin said so in a letter, then spent eleven years explaining it.
bio.evolution.sexual-selection.the-feath.author: author-bio-1
bio.evolution.sexual-selection.the-feath.body:
Writing to Asa Gray on 3 April 1860, four months after the *Origin*:

> "The sight of a feather in a peacock's tail, whenever I gaze at it, makes me sick!"

A tail that heavy, that bright, that expensive should have been deleted by natural selection. His answer arrived in 1871: a second kind of selection, on mates rather than on survival. If peahens prefer the tail, the tail pays — even as its owner pays for it.

bio.evolution.speciation.interbreeds-wit.title: "Interbreeds with" is not transitive, and that is what a species is
bio.evolution.speciation.interbreeds-wit.hook: Walk a ring of salamanders round a valley. Every neighbour interbreeds with the next, and the two ends will not.
bio.evolution.speciation.interbreeds-wit.author: author-bio-1
bio.evolution.speciation.interbreeds-wit.body:
Ensatina salamanders live in a horseshoe of populations around California's Central Valley. Follow the chain north to south down one arm and across the bottom, and each population interbreeds with its neighbour. Where the two arms finally meet in the south, the end forms mostly do not. Greenish warblers do something similar around the Tibetan plateau.

So the question "are these the same species?" gets a yes at every step and a no for the loop. That is not a flaw in the salamanders. It is what you should expect from a category produced by a continuous process: a species is a snapshot of a verb.

Be honest about the examples, though. Genomic work on the warblers confirmed the ring but found historical interruptions in gene flow around it and some mixing where the ends meet, and the salamander case has been argued about for decades. Both survive as rings; neither is the seamless textbook loop, and whether they still "count" depends on how strictly you define the term.
bio.evolution.speciation.interbreeds-wit.rigor:
Mayr's biological species concept (1942) defines species as groups of actually or potentially interbreeding natural populations that are reproductively isolated from other such groups. Written as a relation, "can interbreed with" is meant to sort the living world into disjoint classes.

For that to work, the relation must be an **equivalence relation**: reflexive, symmetric, and *transitive*. Reflexivity and symmetry are free. Transitivity is an empirical claim — that if $A$ interbreeds with $B$ and $B$ with $C$, then $A$ interbreeds with $C$ — and a ring species is a direct counterexample. Without transitivity there are no equivalence classes, so no partition, so no clean species boundaries. The failure is structural, not a measurement problem.

The workarounds are all choices about what to give up. Restrict attention to one place and one time and transitivity is usually restored, which is why field guides work. Or replace the relation with a tree and define species as monophyletic groups, which needs no interbreeding at all and so handles asexual organisms and fossils, at the price of arbitrary cut-offs.

recall.question: Why does a ring species break the biological species concept rather than merely complicate it?

options.text: The relation "can interbreed with" turns out not to be transitive
options.why: without transitivity there are no equivalence classes, so no partition into species at all.

options.text: It shows two species can produce fertile hybrids
options.why: hybrids appear in many pairs; the structural problem is the failure of transitivity around the loop.

options.text: It shows species change over time
options.why: everyone already accepts that; the ring makes trouble in space, at one moment.

options.text: It shows reproductive isolation is impossible to measure
options.why: it is measurable at each contact zone; the measurements simply do not chain.

bio.genetics.central-dogma.crick-picked-.title: Crick picked the wrong word, and biology kept it anyway
bio.genetics.central-dogma.crick-picked-.hook: Crick admitted later that he did not know what 'dogma' meant when he named the most famous rule in biology.
bio.genetics.central-dogma.crick-picked-.author: author-bio-1

reviewed.notes: Diagram caption called reverse transcription "the one real exception", contradicting the card's own rigor (three special transfers). Reworded.

bio.genetics.central-dogma.crick-picked-.body:
He meant something like "a big idea nobody has evidence for yet". He wrote in 1988 that he had not understood that a dogma is a belief that *cannot be doubted*, and that he could just as well have called it the Central Hypothesis.

The idea itself is simple and, unlike the name, careful. DNA is a written record. To use a stretch of it, the cell copies that stretch into RNA — transcription — and a ribosome reads the RNA three letters at a time, adding one amino acid per triplet, building a protein. Sequence in, sequence out, one letter at a time.

The claim is about the *direction*. Information flows from nucleic acid into protein and never back out. A protein cannot dictate a sequence of DNA. That is why an animal's experiences do not get written into its genome, and why Lamarck stays dead: not because acquired traits are absurd, but because there is no machine that could write them down.
bio.genetics.central-dogma.crick-picked-.rigor:
Crick's 1958 statement is sharper than the cartoon arrow chain: once information has passed into protein, it cannot get out again. Transfers between nucleic acids, and from nucleic acid to protein, are possible; transfers from protein to protein or protein to nucleic acid are not.

Sort the nine possible transfers among DNA, RNA and protein into three classes. General, seen in every cell: DNA to DNA, DNA to RNA, RNA to protein. Special, real but restricted: RNA to DNA (reverse transcriptase, used by retroviruses and by your own retrotransposons), RNA to RNA (many RNA viruses), and DNA straight to protein (in cell-free systems). Forbidden, never observed: protein to DNA, protein to RNA, protein to protein.

So reverse transcription, discovered in 1970 and often sold as "the central dogma was wrong", is a *special* transfer that Crick had already allowed. The forbidden row is the one that has never fallen — and it is the row that makes heredity one-directional.

recall.question: Does reverse transcriptase — RNA copied back into DNA — break the central dogma?

options.text: No
options.why: the rule forbids information leaving protein, and Crick listed RNA-to-DNA as a possible special transfer from the start.

options.text: Yes: it reverses the arrow, so the dogma is false as stated
options.why: the dogma was never a claim that arrows only point one way among nucleic acids.

options.text: Yes, but only for viruses; the rule still holds in cells
options.why: your own genome is full of sequences inserted by reverse transcription, so cells do it too.

bio.genetics.crispr.a-scrapbook-of-every.title: Bacteria keep a scrapbook of everyone who ever tried to kill them
bio.genetics.crispr.a-scrapbook-of-every.hook: The gene-editing tool of the decade started as an unexplained pattern of repeats next to a bacterial gene in 1987.
bio.genetics.crispr.a-scrapbook-of-every.author: author-bio-1
bio.genetics.crispr.a-scrapbook-of-every.body:
In 1987 a Japanese team sequencing a gene in *E. coli* found something beside it they could not explain: short repeated sequences, evenly spaced, with a unique chunk of DNA between each pair. Nobody knew what it was for, and nobody much cared for fifteen years.

Francisco Mojica did. In 2005 he showed that the unique chunks match the genomes of phages — the viruses that hunt bacteria. The repeats are a filing cabinet of past attackers. His paper was turned down by four journals before the *Journal of Molecular Evolution* took it.

In 2007 a team working on yoghurt cultures proved the file is operational: a bacterium that survives a phage pastes a piece of it into the array, and its descendants recognise and destroy that phage on sight. Then in 2012 Jinek, Charpentier, Doudna and colleagues showed the recognition step could be reprogrammed — hand the enzyme a synthetic guide and it will cut whatever you name. Nobel in chemistry, 2020.
bio.genetics.crispr.a-scrapbook-of-every.rigor:
Take the type II system, the one that became a tool. A spacer in the array is transcribed into a short **crRNA**, which pairs with a second RNA, the **tracrRNA**; the duplex loads into the protein Cas9 and becomes its instructions.

Cas9 does not scan for the 20-letter match first. It scans for a **protospacer-adjacent motif** — for the *Streptococcus pyogenes* enzyme, the three letters `NGG` — and only where it finds one does it unwind the helix and test the guide against the adjacent 20 bases. A full match gives a blunt double-strand break about 3 base pairs upstream of the motif.

That ordering is the elegant part, and it solves a problem any immune system must solve: how not to attack yourself. The bacterium's own CRISPR array holds the same spacer sequences that the guides encode, but the array does not carry the adjacent motif, so Cas9 never licenses a cut there. Self and non-self are told apart by three letters of context.

The 2012 contribution was to fuse crRNA and tracrRNA into a **single guide RNA**. One synthetic 20-letter sequence, one protein, and the address of a cut anywhere you can name.

recall.question: What stops Cas9 from cutting the bacterium's own CRISPR array, which contains the very sequences it targets?

options.text: The array lacks the short adjacent motif that Cas9 requires before it will unwind and check a match
options.why: self and non-self differ by three letters of context.

options.text: The array is chemically modified so the enzyme cannot bind
options.why: the discrimination is sequence context, not a chemical tag.

options.text: Cas9 is kept physically away from the array
options.why: the protein diffuses through the cell and does encounter it.

options.text: The spacers are stored backwards
options.why: orientation is not what protects them; the missing motif is.
