bio.genetics.dna-structure.it-has-not-es.title: The most under-stated sentence in the history of biology
bio.genetics.dna-structure.it-has-not-es.hook: One page in Nature, two chains, four letters — and the most under-stated sentence anyone has written about heredity.
bio.genetics.dna-structure.it-has-not-es.author: author-bio-1
bio.genetics.dna-structure.it-has-not-es.body:
Watson and Crick's paper in *Nature* on 25 April 1953 fills about a page. Two chains wind around a common axis; adenine always faces thymine, guanine always faces cytosine. Then, rather than claim anything, they close:

> "It has not escaped our notice that the specific pairing we have postulated immediately suggests a possible copying mechanism for the genetic material."

Pull the strands apart and each one is a mould for the other. The shape *was* the mechanism.

Molecular Structure of Nucleic Acids, Nature 171, 737–738

bio.genetics.epigenetics.a-famine-you-ca.title: A famine that ended in 1945, still legible in 2008
bio.genetics.epigenetics.a-famine-you-ca.hook: People conceived in the Dutch famine of 1944 carry a chemical difference sixty years on. The caveats matter as much as the result.
bio.genetics.epigenetics.a-famine-you-ca.author: author-bio-1
bio.genetics.epigenetics.a-famine-you-ca.body:
In the winter of 1944 the western Netherlands was blockaded and rations collapsed. The cohort conceived during those months has been followed ever since, because it is the closest thing to a controlled experiment on prenatal starvation that anyone would tolerate.

In 2008 Heijmans and colleagues compared people conceived at the height of the famine with their own same-sex siblings — the tightest control available — and found about 5% less methylation at a stretch of the *IGF2* gene, six decades later. Only in those exposed around conception. People exposed in late pregnancy showed no methylation difference at all, though their birth weights were lower.

Now the part usually cut from the retelling. It is an association, not an experiment. The effect is small, roughly half a standard deviation, and it is a group average rather than a personal signature. It was measured in blood. And the paper did not show that this chemical difference causes anything.
bio.genetics.epigenetics.a-famine-you-ca.rigor:
A methyl mark is a $\mathrm{CH_3}$ group attached to the 5-carbon of cytosine, almost always where a C is followed by a G. It is not a change to the sequence, which is why "epigenetic" means *above* genetics.

The mark survives cell division by a neat trick. CpG sites are palindromic across the two strands, so after replication each site is *hemimethylated* — marked on the old strand, blank on the new one. The maintenance enzyme DNMT1 reads the old strand and completes the pair. The mark is copied with the DNA, so a liver cell's daughters stay liver cells.

What it does: heavily methylated promoters recruit proteins that compact chromatin and exclude transcription factors, so the gene stays shut.

And here is why "you inherit your grandmother's famine" is mostly not true in mammals. The germ line passes through two near-global waves of demethylation — once in primordial germ cells, once after fertilisation — which wipes the slate. The loci that escape are the *imprinted* ones, where an allele is silenced according to which parent it came from. *IGF2* is imprinted. That is exactly why it is the place to look, and also why it is a special case rather than a general rule.

recall.question: Why is the Dutch famine result usually studied at an imprinted gene like *IGF2*?

options.text: Imprinted loci escape the germ line’s two waves of demethylation
options.why: a mark there can persist when almost every other one has been wiped.

options.text: *IGF2* is the only gene affected by starvation
options.why: plenty of genes respond to nutrition; the question was which marks survive decades.

options.text: Imprinted genes are the only ones that get methylated
options.why: methylation is genome-wide; imprinting is about which parent's copy is silenced.

options.text: Because *IGF2* controls growth, and the famine cohort was small
options.why: the birth-weight effect appeared in the *late*-gestation group, which showed no methylation difference.

bio.genetics.gene-regulation.an-if-state.title: Two Frenchmen found an if-statement inside a bacterium
bio.genetics.gene-regulation.an-if-state.hook: E. coli digests lactose only when there is lactose and no glucose. In 1961 two Frenchmen found the circuit that computes it.
bio.genetics.gene-regulation.an-if-state.author: author-bio-1
bio.genetics.gene-regulation.an-if-state.body:
*E. coli* would rather eat glucose. Give it lactose and no glucose and within minutes it is manufacturing the enzymes that digest lactose; take the lactose away and it stops. The bacterium is running a conditional, and in 1961 François Jacob and Jacques Monod worked out the circuit.

A protein called the repressor sits on a short stretch of DNA right next to the relevant genes and physically blocks the machinery that would copy them. A molecule made from lactose binds the repressor, changes its shape, and knocks it off the DNA. Separately, when glucose runs low a small signalling molecule accumulates and loads an activator that makes the same stretch of DNA far easier to read. Two inputs, one output: transcribe **if** lactose **and not** glucose.

That vocabulary — promoter, repressor, activator, feedback — is the whole of gene regulation. It is also why a liver cell and a neuron, carrying identical genomes, are different animals.
bio.genetics.gene-regulation.an-if-state.rigor:
The operon is the unit: three structural genes (*lacZ*, *lacY*, *lacA*) sharing one promoter and transcribed into a single messenger RNA. Upstream sits the *operator*, a binding site; elsewhere on the chromosome, *lacI* encodes the repressor that binds it.

Jacob and Monod's decisive experiments were merodiploids — cells carrying two copies of the region, one mutant — and they established the distinction that makes molecular genetics possible. The repressor is **trans-acting**: it is a diffusible protein, so a good copy anywhere in the cell rescues a broken copy elsewhere. The operator is **cis-acting**: it is a site on the DNA and it governs only the genes physically attached to it, so a broken operator cannot be rescued by a good one on the other chromosome. Trans means "a molecule"; cis means "an address".

The circuit also has feedback. One of the genes, *lacY*, builds the permease that imports lactose, so induction raises the input that caused it. The loop makes the response all-or-none rather than graded: in a population under weak induction you see fully induced cells and fully uninduced cells, not intermediate ones — a result Novick and Weiner reported in 1957, before anyone knew what an operon was.

recall.question: A mutation in the operator cannot be rescued by a good copy of the operator on a second chromosome in the same cell. Why?

options.text: The operator is a site on the DNA, not a product
options.why: it can only control the genes physically attached to it, which is what "cis-acting" means.

options.text: Because the operator makes a protein that cannot diffuse
options.why: the operator encodes nothing; the diffusible product is the repressor, from *lacI*.

options.text: Because bacteria have only one chromosome
options.why: they can be made partially diploid, and that is exactly how the experiment was done.

options.text: Because the second copy is silenced
options.why: both copies are transcribed; the point is that control is local to the DNA molecule.

sources.title: Genetic regulatory mechanisms in the synthesis of proteins, Journal of Molecular Biology 3, 318–356
sources.author: François Jacob and Jacques Monod

bio.genetics.mendel.the-monks-peas.title: The monk's peas saved an argument Darwin never knew was broken
bio.genetics.mendel.the-monks-peas.hook: If inheritance blended like paint, natural selection would run out of material in ten generations. Darwin never learned why it does not.
bio.genetics.mendel.the-monks-peas.author: author-bio-1
bio.genetics.mendel.the-monks-peas.body:
In 1867 a Scottish engineer named Fleeming Jenkin reviewed the *Origin* and pointed at a hole. Suppose inheritance blends, as nearly everyone then assumed, so that a child is the average of its parents. Then any new variant is halved every generation. After ten generations it is a thousandth of itself. Selection would arrive to find nothing left to select.

Darwin worried about this for the rest of his life. The answer had already been printed, in 1866, in the proceedings of a natural history society in Brünn, by an Augustinian friar counting peas.

Mendel's point is that inheritance is not paint. It is cards. Cross a tall plant with a short one and the offspring are tall, but they still hold the short card, unchanged, and a quarter of the *grand*children come out short again. Nothing is averaged. Nothing is diluted. Variation is stored, not blended away.

That repairs Darwin's third premise, and immediately raises a harder question: if transmission by itself changes nothing, what does a population of cards do when nobody is pushing it?
bio.genetics.mendel.the-monks-peas.rigor:
Blending, made precise. If an offspring's trait is $z_o=\tfrac12(z_m+z_f)$ with parents drawn independently from a population of variance $V$, then

$$\operatorname{Var}(z_o)=\tfrac14\left(V+V\right)=V/2 .$$

So $V_t = V_0\,2^{-t}$: variance dies exponentially. Selection consumes variance and blending manufactures none, which is why Jenkin's objection had teeth.

Particulate inheritance loses nothing. Mendel's law of segregation says a diploid parent carrying $A$ and $a$ puts one of them into each gamete, each with probability $\tfrac12$, and copies it exactly. His law of independent assortment adds that alleles at different loci are transmitted independently — true for loci on different chromosomes, and Mendel was lucky in his choice of traits.

The 3:1 ratio is then just two fair coins. The cross $Aa \times Aa$ gives $AA$, $Aa$, $aA$, $aa$ each with probability $\tfrac14$, and if $A$ is dominant, three of the four look identical. Across his seven traits Mendel counted 14,949 dominant to 5,010 recessive: 2.98 to 1.

Cards, not paint. Next: what a population of cards does when left alone.

recall.question: Why would blending inheritance have destroyed Darwin's argument?

options.text: It halves the population's variance every generation, so novel variants fade away before selection can amplify them
options.why: no variation, no selection.

options.text: It makes offspring identical to their parents, so nothing new ever appears
options.why: blending does the opposite: it averages away what is new.

options.text: It prevents dominant traits from spreading
options.why: dominance is about how a genotype looks, not about whether a variant persists.

options.text: It makes inheritance random rather than faithful
options.why: the problem is not noise, it is the systematic shrinkage of differences.

sources.title: Experiments on Plant Hybridization (Versuche über Pflanzen-Hybriden)
sources.author: Gregor Mendel

bio.genetics.mutation.how-many-typos.title: How many typos did you start life with?
bio.genetics.mutation.how-many-typos.hook: You were born carrying single-letter changes that neither of your parents had. Guess the order of magnitude before you read on.
bio.genetics.mutation.how-many-typos.author: author-bio-1
bio.genetics.mutation.how-many-typos.body:
Three billion letters had to be copied to make each of the cells you began as, and copying is never perfect. So: how many single-letter changes do you carry that neither of your parents had? Pick an order of magnitude — ten, a hundred, a thousand, a million.

Then the harder question, the one with an actual mechanism behind it. Did more of those new mutations come from your mother or from your father? And what would you have to know about your parents to sharpen the estimate?

recall.question: How many new mutations, and from which parent?
recall.answer: Around 60–70. Sequencing 78 Icelandic parent–child trios, Kong et al. (2012) measured about 1.2 × 10⁻⁸ new mutations per base per generation — roughly 63 per child when the father was 29.7. Most come from the father: sperm are produced by continuing cell division throughout life while a woman's eggs are not, so the count rises by about two mutations for every extra year of the father's age.

sources.title: Rate of de novo mutations and the importance of father's age to disease risk, Nature 488, 471–475
sources.author: Augustine Kong et al.

bio.genetics.population-genetics.the-the.title: The theorem that says nothing happens
bio.genetics.population-genetics.the-the.hook: A pure mathematician settled biology's loudest argument of 1908 with one line of algebra, and apologised for intruding.
bio.genetics.population-genetics.the-the.author: author-bio-1

reviewed.notes: Yule's objection is documented as dominants spreading until they swamp recessives; the brown-eyes/blue-eyes version is not in the cited sources. Hardy's opening quote verified verbatim.

bio.genetics.population-genetics.the-the.body:
In 1908 the geneticist Reginald Punnett could not answer an objection. Udny Yule had argued that a dominant allele ought to spread through a population until it had swamped the recessive one — so either Mendel was wrong or the world was. Punnett took the problem to his cricket partner, the Cambridge pure mathematician G. H. Hardy.

Hardy's letter to *Science* opens: "I am reluctant to intrude in a discussion concerning matters of which I have no expert knowledge, and I should have expected the very simple point which I wish to make to have been familiar to biologists."

The very simple point: dominance says how a genotype *looks*, not how common it is. Under random mating, allele frequencies do not change at all, and genotype frequencies reach their resting values after a single generation and stay. Wilhelm Weinberg published the same thing in German that year, which is why the name has two halves.

What you are looking at is biology's null hypothesis — the sound of nothing happening. Every interesting thing in evolution is a departure from it.
bio.genetics.population-genetics.the-the.rigor:
Let alleles $A$ and $a$ have frequencies $p$ and $q$ with $p+q=1$. Assume random mating, no selection, no mutation, no migration, infinite population, non-overlapping generations.

A zygote is two gametes drawn independently, so

$$f(AA)=p^{2},\qquad f(Aa)=2pq,\qquad f(aa)=q^{2},$$

which sum to $(p+q)^{2}=1$. Now compute the next generation's allele frequency: $p' = p^{2} + \tfrac12(2pq) = p(p+q) = p$. Nothing moves. One round of random mating and the population is frozen, whatever it started from.

So every evolutionary force is a named violation of one assumption. Selection breaks "no selection"; finite size breaks "infinite" and gives you drift; inbreeding and assortative mating break "random". Population structure breaks it in a useful way: pool two populations with different $p$ and you observe *fewer* heterozygotes than $2pq$. That deficit is the Wahlund effect, and it lets you detect hidden structure in a sample without being told it is there.

To test a real sample, compare observed counts against $Np^{2}$, $2Npq$, $Nq^{2}$ with $\chi^{2}=\sum (O-E)^{2}/E$ on one degree of freedom: three genotypes minus two allele frequencies.

A population at equilibrium is a population nothing has pushed. Next: what pushes.

recall.question: A population is found to have far fewer heterozygotes than $2pq$. What is the most informative first guess?

options.text: The sample pools two or more groups with different allele frequencies
options.why: the Wahlund effect, a deficit of heterozygotes that reveals hidden structure.

options.text: The allele is dominant, so heterozygotes are hidden
options.why: dominance changes what you see in the phenotype, not the genotype counts.

options.text: Natural selection is favouring the $A$ allele
options.why: directional selection shifts $p$ itself; it does not by itself produce a heterozygote deficit.

options.text: The population is too large for the model
options.why: the model's trouble is small populations, where drift moves frequencies around.

sources.title: Mendelian Proportions in a Mixed Population, Science 28(706), 49–50
sources.author: G. H. Hardy

bio.genetics.sequencing-genomics.what-di.title: What did it cost to read one human genome in 2001?
bio.genetics.sequencing-genomics.what-di.hook: One curve in biology outran Moore's law for years. Guess the numbers before you look.
bio.genetics.sequencing-genomics.what-di.author: author-bio-1
bio.genetics.sequencing-genomics.what-di.body:
The Human Genome Project took thirteen years and roughly \$2.7 billion, but that budget covered technology development, model organisms and ethics work as well as sequencing. The cleaner question is the one the US National Human Genome Research Institute has tracked ever since: the production cost of sequencing *one more* human genome, start to finish, at a funded centre.

Three guesses. What was it in September 2001? What was it two decades later? And what happened between October 2007 and January 2008 that made this the one technology curve people compare favourably to Moore's law?

recall.question: The three numbers.
recall.answer: September 2001: \$95,263,072. May 2022: \$524.63 — a factor of roughly 180,000 in twenty-one years. The jump: October 2007 was the last Sanger data point at \$7.1 million; by January 2008, with centres switched to next-generation sequencers, it was \$3.1 million, and NHGRI describes what followed as a "sudden and profound out-pacing of Moore's Law". Caveat: these are production costs at funded centres, not a price you could pay, and they exclude interpreting what the sequence means.

sources.title: The Cost of Sequencing a Human Genome (NHGRI)

bio.history.biology-and-math.mendels-dat.title: Mendel's data are too good to be true
bio.history.biology-and-math.mendels-dat.hook: Fisher did not ask whether Mendel's peas fit the theory. He asked whether they fit it too well, and computed the odds.
bio.history.biology-and-math.mendels-dat.author: author-bio-1

reviewed.notes: Event date corrected to the paper's 15 April 1936. Fisher's "once in twenty-nine trials" and "falsified to agree closely" both verified verbatim via Hartl and Fairbanks 2007.

bio.history.biology-and-math.mendels-dat.body:
In 1936 Ronald Fisher went back through the pea counts, carrying the statistics he had largely invented himself. His question was new. Not *do these data fit the theory* — everyone agreed they did. Do they fit it **too well**?

Real sampling is noisy. Flip a thousand fair coins and you land near five hundred, not on it. Mendel's ratios hug the predicted values across experiment after experiment, more snugly than chance permits: pooled, the chi-squared statistic came out implausibly *small*, and of one series Fisher wrote that "a deviation as fortunate as Mendel's is to be expected once in twenty-nine trials". His verdict was careful and brutal: the data "have been falsified to agree closely with Mendel's expectations" — possibly, he allowed, by an assistant who knew what answer was wanted.

The argument has run for ninety years. Re-analyses since — Hartl and Fairbanks in 2007, a book-length reassessment in 2008 — conclude there is no good case that Mendel fabricated anything.

What makes this a card about mathematics rather than gossip: you can only detect data that are too good if you have a model of how noisy honest data should be.

recall.question: What was Fisher's actual argument against Mendel's counts, and what is the current verdict?
recall.answer: Not that the ratios were wrong but that they were too close to the predicted values — pooled across his experiments the chi-squared statistic came out implausibly small, which is what an honest sample almost never does. After re-analyses by Hartl and Fairbanks (2007) and a book-length reassessment in 2008, the consensus is that deliberate fabrication is not supported; unconscious bias in classifying ambiguous peas is the most defended reading.

sources.title: Has Mendel's work been rediscovered?, Annals of Science 1, 115–137
sources.author: Ronald A. Fisher

sources.title: Mud Sticks: On the Alleged Falsification of Mendel’s Data, Genetics 175(3), 975–979
sources.author: Daniel L. Hartl and Daniel J. Fairbanks

bio.history.biology-and-math.one-line-th.title: One line that holds all of Darwin
bio.history.biology-and-math.one-line-th.hook: An outsider with no training in genetics wrote one line that contains selection, transmission and Darwin's entire argument.
bio.history.biology-and-math.one-line-th.author: author-bio-1

reviewed.notes: Price did not sell his house; he moved on a thyroid-surgery insurance payout in November 1967. Corrected, which also makes the story sharper.

bio.history.biology-and-math.one-line-th.body:
George Price came to London in November 1967 with no training in genetics. He was an American chemist who had worked on the Manhattan Project and then at IBM on early computer-aided design. Thyroid surgery in 1966 had left his shoulder partly paralysed; he took the medical insurance money, moved countries, and chased an idea about why anything is ever kind to anything else. University College gave him a desk. By 1970 he had a paper in *Nature* that reorganised how biologists argue about selection.

It is one line, and it assumes almost nothing — no genes, no diploidy, no particular way of reproducing. It splits the change in any average trait into two accounts: how much *selection* moved it, and how much *transmission* moved it.

His own story ends badly. Price converted to Christianity in 1970, gave away nearly everything he owned to homeless people in London, and took his own life in January 1975. The equation outlived him and is now the standard way to ask whether an apparent benefit to a group is really selection on groups.
bio.history.biology-and-math.one-line-th.rigor:
Index individuals by $i$, with trait $z_i$ and fitness $w_i$ (number of offspring). Let $z_i'$ be the mean trait among $i$'s offspring and $\Delta z_i = z_i' - z_i$. Then, exactly,

$$\bar{w}\,\Delta\bar{z} \;=\; \operatorname{Cov}(w_i, z_i) \;+\; \mathbb{E}\!\left[w_i\,\Delta z_i\right].$$

This is an identity, not a model. It follows from the definitions of mean and covariance, so it cannot be false; it can only be uninformative. The first term is selection: the covariance between carrying the trait and leaving offspring. The second is transmission: mutation, meiotic drive, any way offspring fail to be copies.

Now read episode 1's three conditions off the right-hand side as three ways to make it vanish. If $z$ does not vary, the covariance is zero. If $w$ does not depend on $z$, the covariance is zero. If offspring do not resemble parents, the transmission term erases whatever selection did. Darwin's three facts and one conclusion are the claim that this right-hand side is not zero.

Apply it twice, nesting individuals inside groups, and the first term becomes the covariance between group fitness and group trait, the second the average within-group Price term. That is what multilevel selection means, written down.

recall.question: Why can the Price equation never be wrong, and what makes it useful anyway?
recall.answer: It is an algebraic identity that follows from the definitions of mean, covariance and expectation, so no data can contradict it. Its use is bookkeeping: it forces you to say exactly how much of a change is covariance between fitness and trait (selection) and how much is imperfect transmission — and, nested, it defines what selection on groups actually means.

bio.history.dna-race.photo-51-told-prope.title: Photo 51, told properly
bio.history.dna-race.photo-51-told-prope.hook: The famous X-ray was taken in May 1952. What Franklin had already worked out from it matters more than who showed it to whom.
bio.history.dna-race.photo-51-told-prope.author: author-bio-1
bio.history.dna-race.photo-51-told-prope.body:
On 2 May 1952 Raymond Gosling, working under Rosalind Franklin at King's College London, exposed an X-ray film of a DNA fibre held at high humidity. The result is a blurred X of spots. That X is the signature of a helix, and the spacings give you the pitch and the diameter.

The popular telling turns Franklin into a technician who took a photograph she did not understand. She was a crystallographer, she had already established that the phosphate backbone faces outward, and she had determined the crystal symmetry — which by itself implies the two strands run in opposite directions.

What actually happened is smaller and worse. In January 1953 Maurice Wilkins showed the photograph to James Watson without asking her. Separately, Max Perutz passed Watson and Crick an unpublished Medical Research Council progress report containing her measurements. Neither act was theft in any legal sense. Neither was requested.

Franklin died of ovarian cancer in 1958, aged 37. The Nobel was awarded in 1962, and it is not given posthumously — so the question of whether she would have shared it has no answer, only an argument.

recall.question: What is the most accurate description of Rosalind Franklin's role?

options.text: A crystallographer whose own analysis had fixed key structural facts
options.why: and whose unpublished data reached Watson and Crick without her knowledge.

options.text: A technician who produced an image she was not equipped to interpret
options.why: she had already derived the backbone's position and the crystal symmetry from her data.

options.text: A rival who independently solved the double helix first
options.why: she was moving towards it but had not assembled the model when Watson and Crick published.

options.text: A collaborator who was fully credited at the time
options.why: the 1953 paper thanks King's College in general terms; her specific data are not acknowledged.

sources.title: Molecular Structure of Nucleic Acids: A Structure for Deoxyribose Nucleic Acid

bio.history.latam.el-medico-que-tenia-ra.title: El médico que tenía razón veinte años antes
bio.history.latam.el-medico-que-tenia-ra.hook: En 1881 Finlay dijo cuál mosquito transmitía la fiebre amarilla. Tuvieron que pasar casi veinte años para que le creyeran.
bio.history.latam.el-medico-que-tenia-ra.author: author-bio-1
bio.history.latam.el-medico-que-tenia-ra.body:
El 14 de agosto de 1881 Carlos Juan Finlay leyó ante la Real Academia de Ciencias Médicas, Físicas y Naturales de La Habana un trabajo cuyo título ya decía todo: «El mosquito hipotéticamente considerado como agente de transmisión de la fiebre amarilla». Seis meses antes había presentado la idea en una conferencia sanitaria internacional en Washington y lo habían oído con frialdad. Esta vez unos sonrieron, otros murmuraron, otros salieron del salón.

La propuesta era extrañísima para la época. La enfermedad no viajaba en el aire viciado ni en la ropa de los enfermos: viajaba dentro de un insecto específico, el *Culex fasciatus* —hoy *Aedes aegypti*—, y en la hembra. Entre cientos de especies posibles, Finlay señaló la correcta.

Pasaron casi veinte años. En 1900 la comisión del ejército estadounidense dirigida por Walter Reed llegó a La Habana, repitió los experimentos y confirmó la hipótesis. Uno de sus miembros, Jesse Lazear, murió de fiebre amarilla el 25 de septiembre de ese año, contagiado durante el trabajo.

La idea no cambió. Cambió quién la firmaba.

recall.question: ¿Qué hacía tan difícil de aceptar la hipótesis de Finlay en 1881?

options.text: Proponía un vector vivo y específico en vez de miasmas
options.why: había que creerle a un médico que señalaba una especie concreta de mosquito entre cientos.

options.text: Nadie sabía todavía que existían los microorganismos
options.why: Pasteur y Koch ya estaban establecidos; lo raro era el intermediario que los transportaba.

options.text: Finlay no hizo experimentos
options.why: hizo más de un centenar de inoculaciones con mosquitos durante esos años; lo que faltó fue credibilidad, no trabajo.

options.text: La fiebre amarilla era poco común en Cuba
options.why: era endémica y devastadora, y por eso mismo el problema era urgente.

bio.history.microscope-cell-theory.the-w.title: The word "cell" is not about monks
bio.history.microscope-cell-theory.the-w.hook: Hooke compared them to a honeycomb. The story about monks' rooms is a later invention that everyone repeats.
bio.history.microscope-cell-theory.the-w.author: author-bio-1

reviewed.notes: Leeuwenhoek's rainwater animalcules were 1676; the dental scrapings were 1683. Split the two dates. Monks'-cells myth confirmed against Peters 2024, Plant Cell 36(11).

bio.history.microscope-cell-theory.the-w.body:
In January 1665 Robert Hooke published *Micrographia*, sliced cork thin enough to see through, and found it built of tiny empty boxes. He called them cells.

The story you were told — that he named them after monks' sleeping rooms — is not in the book. Hooke's own comparison is a honeycomb, and "cell" was already ordinary anatomical vocabulary for a small chamber. The monastery version is a nineteenth-century embellishment that survives because it is charming and because it flattered cell theory.

What Hooke saw, in any case, were the dead walls of plant cells. Living ones arrived a decade later from Delft, where a draper named Antonie van Leeuwenhoek ground lenses better than anyone in Europe and wrote to the Royal Society in 1676 about little animals swimming in rainwater, and in 1683 about the ones in his own dental scrapings. The Society did not believe him at first. He never revealed his lens-making method, and nobody reproduced it for centuries.

Two men, two decades, and the observation that biology would eventually be rebuilt on: everything alive is made of these, and every one of them comes from another one.

recall.question: Where does the word "cell" in biology actually come from?

options.text: Hooke's 1665 description of cork
options.why: "cell" was already standard vocabulary for a small chamber, and his own comparison was to a honeycomb.

options.text: From the Latin for monks' sleeping rooms, as Hooke explained in *Micrographia*
options.why: the book contains no monks and no such explanation.

options.text: From Leeuwenhoek's Dutch term for the little animals he saw
options.why: he described swimming organisms, not compartments, and wrote in Dutch.

options.text: From nineteenth-century German cell theory
options.why: Schleiden and Schwann inherited the word; they did not coin it.

sources.title: Will the real Robert Hooke please stand up?, The Plant Cell 36(11), 4680
sources.author: Winfried S. Peters

bio.history.origin-of-life.a-jar-of-gas-.title: A jar of gas, a spark, and amino acids by Friday
bio.history.origin-of-life.a-jar-of-gas-.hook: A graduate student sealed four gases in glass, ran sparks through them for a week, and found the building blocks of protein.
bio.history.origin-of-life.a-jar-of-gas-.author: author-bio-1
bio.history.origin-of-life.a-jar-of-gas-.body:
In 1952 a graduate student named Stanley Miller talked Harold Urey into letting him try something nobody thought would work. He sealed water, methane, ammonia and hydrogen into glass tubing, boiled the water so the vapour circulated, and fired continuous electric sparks through it to stand in for lightning. He left it running.

Within a week the water had gone pink-brown. In it were amino acids — the units proteins are built from — assembled out of nothing but gas and electricity. The paper appeared in *Science* in 1953, the same year as the double helix.

Two honest corrections. Current models say the early atmosphere was probably much less hospitable to that chemistry than Miller assumed: mostly carbon dioxide and nitrogen rather than methane and ammonia. So his particular recipe is probably not Earth's. And a coda in his favour: he kept his sealed vials, and a re-analysis in 2008 with modern instruments found far more amino acids than 1950s methods could detect.

What still nobody has done is get from a soup of parts to something that copies itself. That, not the parts, is the problem.

recall.question: What did the Miller–Urey experiment actually establish?

options.text: That the building blocks of life form spontaneously from simple gases and an energy source
options.why: no special chemistry required to make the parts.

options.text: That life arose in a warm pond on the early Earth
options.why: it showed a chemistry is possible, not that it is what happened.

options.text: That the early atmosphere contained methane and ammonia
options.why: that was Miller's assumption, and current models say it was probably wrong.

options.text: That self-replicating molecules can arise from gas
options.why: no replicator appeared; getting from parts to a copier is still the open problem.

sources.title: A Production of Amino Acids Under Possible Primitive Earth Conditions, Science 117, 528–529
sources.author: Stanley L. Miller

bio.neuro.brain-map.the-map-with-enormou.title: The map of your body in your head has enormous lips
bio.neuro.brain-map.the-map-with-enormou.hook: There is a map of your body in your cortex, and its hands and lips are grotesquely oversized. That distortion is the useful part.
bio.neuro.brain-map.the-map-with-enormou.author: author-bio-1
bio.neuro.brain-map.the-map-with-enormou.body:
In the 1930s Wilder Penfield operated on people with severe epilepsy while they were awake. The scalp takes local anaesthetic and the brain itself feels nothing, so he could touch a stimulating electrode to the exposed cortex and ask what the patient noticed. Here, and the thumb tingles. Two millimetres over, and it is the index finger. He was trying to find tissue he could safely remove; what he got was a map.

Running down a strip of cortex, the body is laid out in order — but with the proportions wrong. Lips, tongue and hands occupy huge territories; the trunk and the thigh get slivers. Cortex is handed out according to how finely a part must be sensed and controlled, not by how big it is. Your fingertips are expensive; your back is cheap.

The clean little figure in textbooks oversells it. Penfield himself noted heavy overlap between regions, and precision scanning in 2023 found the strip is interrupted by patches that belong to a whole-body action network rather than to any single limb.

recall.question: Why do the hands and lips take up so much of the cortical map?

options.text: Cortical area tracks the precision of sensing and control a part needs, not its physical size
options.why: fingertips and lips are high-resolution instruments.

options.text: Because they contain the most muscle
options.why: the thigh has far more muscle and gets a sliver of cortex.

options.text: Because they are closest to the brain
options.why: the face is nearer than the foot, but the map is not organised by distance.

options.text: Because they are used most often
options.why: the trunk is in constant use and barely registers; resolution is what buys cortex.

sources.title: Somatic Motor and Sensory Representation in the Cerebral Cortex of Man as Studied by Electrical Stimulation, Brain 60(4), 389–443
sources.author: Wilder Penfield and Edwin Boldrey

sources.title: A somato-cognitive action network alternates with effector regions in motor cortex, Nature 617, 351–359
sources.author: Evan M. Gordon et al.

bio.neuro.decision-making.a-sequential-t.title: Your brain may be running a test Wald wrote down in 1945
bio.neuro.decision-making.a-sequential-t.hook: Wald's 1945 test for deciding when you have seen enough data has a candidate implementation in parietal cortex.
bio.neuro.decision-making.a-sequential-t.author: author-bio-1

reviewed.notes: Difficulty 2 to 3: the rigor is Wald's SPRT plus drift-diffusion first-passage closed forms, on a par with the other level-3 cards in the shard.

bio.neuro.decision-making.a-sequential-t.body:
Show someone a cloud of flickering dots with a weak net drift and ask which way it moves. Give them longer and they do better; push them to answer fast and they do worse. That trade-off has a shape, and the shape is the interesting thing: it is what you would get from a decision-maker who keeps collecting evidence until it has enough, rather than one who looks once and guesses.

Record from parietal cortex in a monkey doing exactly this task and the firing rate climbs during the trial. The steeper the climb, the stronger the motion; and the eye movement comes roughly when the rate reaches the same level, whatever the motion strength. That is what accumulating evidence towards a fixed bound looks like from the outside.

Say "consistent with", not "is". Single-trial analyses have argued the ramps are really abrupt steps, and switching the region off barely changes behaviour. The neurons are a candidate implementation of the algorithm, not a proof of it.

The algorithm, though, is not a guess.
bio.neuro.decision-making.a-sequential-t.rigor:
Wald's **sequential probability ratio test**: accumulate the log-likelihood ratio of your two hypotheses as evidence arrives,

$$\Lambda_n=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\log\frac{p(x_i\mid H_1)}{p(x_i\mid H_0)},$$

and stop the first time $\Lambda_n$ leaves $[\,\log\frac{\beta}{1-\alpha},\ \log\frac{1-\beta}{\alpha}\,]$. Wald and Wolfowitz proved in 1948 that this minimises the expected number of samples for given error rates $\alpha,\beta$ — no other test decides faster at that accuracy.

In continuous time with Gaussian noise this is the **drift–diffusion model**: $dx=\mu\,dt+\sigma\,dW$ with absorbing boundaries at $\pm a$, starting at $0$. It has closed forms,

$$P(\text{correct})=\frac{1}{1+e^{-2a\mu/\sigma^{2}}},\qquad \mathbb{E}[T]=\frac{a}{\mu}\tanh\!\left(\frac{a\mu}{\sigma^{2}}\right),$$

so the whole speed–accuracy trade-off is one curve traced by the single parameter $a$. Raising the bound buys accuracy at a cost in time, and the exchange rate is fixed by the signal-to-noise ratio $\mu/\sigma$. "Being careful" is not a personality trait here; it is a number.

Optimality is narrower than the fame suggests: two alternatives, stationary independent evidence, accuracy as the objective. With more options, drifting evidence, or a reward-rate objective, the plain bounded accumulator stops being optimal.

recall.question: In the drift–diffusion account, what does a person change when they decide to "be more careful"?

options.text: The height of the decision bound $a$
options.why: raising it demands more accumulated evidence, buying accuracy at a predictable cost in time.

options.text: The drift rate $\mu$
options.why: that is set by the stimulus and the quality of their senses, not by choice.

options.text: The noise $\sigma$
options.why: internal noise is not under voluntary control; only the stopping rule is.

options.text: Which hypothesis they start from
options.why: the model starts unbiased at zero; a prior shifts the starting point, which is a separate knob.

bio.neuro.neural-coding.ninety-bits-a-se.title: Remember entropy? A fly's neuron carries about 90 bits a second
bio.neuro.neural-coding.ninety-bits-a-se.hook: Entropy told you how much a message could say. Point it at a fly's spike train and you get a number: about 90 bits a second.
bio.neuro.neural-coding.ninety-bits-a-se.author: author-bio-1

reviewed.notes: Dropped an unsupported claim (rates "double from 25 ms to sub-millisecond"): Strong et al. scan 800 ms to 2 ms, entropy rate rising ~40x at ~50% efficiency. 90 bits/s and 0.5-2 bits/spike verified.

bio.neuro.neural-coding.ninety-bits-a-se.body:
Entropy measured how much a distribution could surprise you: the average number of yes/no questions needed to pin down an outcome. A spike train is a message written in that alphabet — spike, no spike, at some time resolution — so the same machinery applies without modification, and it gives a number.

The recipe is beautifully direct. Show a fly a moving visual scene and record one motion-sensitive neuron. Chop the spike train into short words. Measure how much variety the words show over the whole recording: that is the total entropy, the neuron's full vocabulary. Then replay exactly the same scene over and over and measure how much variety remains: that is noise, the part of the vocabulary the stimulus does not control. Subtract.

What is left is information, and for the blowfly's H1 neuron it runs up to about 90 bits per second, roughly one to two bits per spike — within about a factor of two of the ceiling set by the spike train's own entropy.

One honest warning before the arithmetic: bits per spike is not a constant of nature.
bio.neuro.neural-coding.ninety-bits-a-se.rigor:
Write $R$ for the response word and $S$ for the stimulus. With words built as binary vectors over $T/\Delta\tau$ bins,

$$H(R)=-\sum_r p(r)\log_2 p(r), \qquad H(R\mid S)=\Big\langle -\sum_r p(r\mid s)\log_2 p(r\mid s)\Big\rangle_s,$$

$$I(R;S)=H(R)-H(R\mid S).$$

$H(R)$ is estimated from the whole recording, $H(R\mid S)$ from repeated presentations of the identical stimulus at matched times. Both are biased upward by finite sampling, so you extrapolate in $1/N$, and both depend on $T$, so you extrapolate the rates in $1/T$.

Two consequences worth carrying. First, $I(R;S)\le H(R)$: a neuron can never transmit more than the entropy of its own spike train, which makes "efficiency" $I/H(R)$ a meaningful quantity — and H1 runs at roughly half of its own ceiling.

Second, the numbers are conditional on your choices. Finer $\Delta\tau$ reveals more structure and raises the estimate: across the range Strong and colleagues scanned, 800 ms bins down to 2 ms, the spike train's own entropy rate climbs by a factor of about forty, and the information climbs roughly in step — efficiency stays near half the whole way. Different stimulus statistics then move bits per spike from about 0.5 to about 2 in the very same neuron. Information is a property of the channel *and* of what you send down it — which is exactly what entropy said in the first place.

recall.question: In the direct method, what does subtracting the noise entropy from the total entropy accomplish?

options.text: It removes the variability the stimulus does not control, leaving only the variety that actually depends on the input
options.why: that residual is the information.

options.text: It corrects for the neuron's background firing rate
options.why: rate is already inside both terms; what is removed is trial-to-trial unreliability.

options.text: It converts the spike count into bits
options.why: the count becomes bits as soon as you build word distributions; the subtraction is about reliability.

options.text: It compensates for finite sampling bias
options.why: real, but handled separately by extrapolating in the number of samples.

bio.neuro.neurons.everything-we-know-cam.title: Everything we know about nerves, we learned from a squid
bio.neuro.neurons.everything-we-know-cam.hook: A squid grew a nerve fibre a thousand times fatter than yours, for reasons of its own. Neuroscience has been living off it ever since.
bio.neuro.neurons.everything-we-know-cam.author: author-bio-1
bio.neuro.neurons.everything-we-know-cam.body:
In 1936 J. Z. Young took a second look at a pale tube running down the inside of a squid's mantle. He had assumed it was a blood vessel, because nothing that wide could be a nerve fibre. It was a nerve fibre — a single one, up to a millimetre and a half across, perhaps a thousand times the diameter of the ones in your arm. (L. W. Williams had described them in 1909; the work was forgotten, and Williams died in a lift accident three years later.)

The squid has it for speed. Fat axons conduct faster, and the animal uses this one to fire the escape jet that gets it away from a fish.

Fat also means you can push a wire *inside* it. That is what Hodgkin and Huxley did at Plymouth from 1939: they recorded the voltage across a living membrane from within the cell. Every textbook picture of how a nerve fires comes out of an animal that evolved a giant nerve for a reason that had nothing to do with us.

recall.question: Why was the squid giant axon the breakthrough preparation for electrophysiology?
recall.answer: Because it is enormous — up to about 1.5 mm across. That is wide enough to insert an electrode inside a single living axon and clamp or measure the voltage across its membrane directly, which no ordinary neuron allowed at the time.

bio.neuro.neurons.four-equations-that-fi.title: Four equations that make a nerve fire
bio.neuro.neurons.four-equations-that-fi.hook: Four coupled nonlinear ODEs, fitted in 1952, predicted the shape and the speed of a nerve impulse before anyone knew channels were proteins.
bio.neuro.neurons.four-equations-that-fi.author: author-bio-1

reviewed.notes: HH's rest state is globally attracting, so the "threshold" is not a basin boundary. Replaced with FitzHugh's quasi-threshold, in the rigor and in the recall distractor.

bio.neuro.neurons.four-equations-that-fi.body:
A nerve impulse is not electricity running down a wire. It is a chain reaction of gates, and the chain reaction is what makes it regenerate itself instead of fading out like a signal in a cable.

Raise the voltage across the membrane a little and sodium gates open. Sodium ions pour in, which raises the voltage further, which opens more gates. That positive feedback is the upstroke, and it is why the spike is all-or-nothing: once it starts it runs to completion. Then two slower processes catch up. The sodium gates inactivate — a separate mechanism from the one that opened them — and potassium gates open and let positive charge leave. The voltage overshoots downward, and the cell sits briefly refractory before it can do it again.

Hodgkin and Huxley measured those conductances in the squid axon under voltage clamp, fitted curves to them, and turned the whole story into a system of differential equations that reproduced the spike, and its conduction velocity, on a hand calculator.
bio.neuro.neurons.four-equations-that-fi.rigor:
One equation for the membrane and three for the gates:

$$C_m\frac{dV}{dt}=I-\bar{g}_{\mathrm{K}}n^{4}(V-V_{\mathrm{K}})-\bar{g}_{\mathrm{Na}}m^{3}h(V-V_{\mathrm{Na}})-\bar{g}_{L}(V-V_{L}),$$

$$\frac{dx}{dt}=\alpha_x(V)\,(1-x)-\beta_x(V)\,x,\qquad x\in\{n,m,h\}.$$

Each gating variable is a probability in $[0,1]$, relaxing towards a voltage-dependent target. The exponents encode a guess: $n^{4}$ says a potassium channel conducts only when four independent particles are all in place; $m^{3}h$ says sodium needs three activating particles *and* one non-inactivating one. Hodgkin and Huxley chose those powers to fit curves. Decades later, structural work found potassium channels really are tetramers.

The nonlinearity lives in $\alpha_x,\beta_x$, which depend on $V$, so the equations feed back on themselves. The rest state is stable: small perturbations decay. Large ones do not — they escape into a stereotyped excursion and return. That is **excitability**, and the "threshold" is neither a bifurcation nor a true separatrix: with no applied current every trajectory eventually returns to rest, so what looks like a threshold is a very steep but continuous transition — FitzHugh's *quasi-threshold*. Which is why reduced two-variable versions like FitzHugh–Nagumo reproduce the whole behaviour with a cubic nullcline and nothing else.

Add a spatial term, $C_m\partial_t V = \frac{a}{2R}\partial^2_x V - \sum I_{\text{ion}}$, and the system supports a travelling wave whose speed the 1952 paper predicted correctly. Nobel Prize, 1963.

recall.question: What makes the action potential all-or-nothing rather than proportional to the stimulus?

options.text: Sodium entry raises the voltage, which opens more sodium gates
options.why: positive feedback that runs to completion once the rest state's basin is escaped.

options.text: A hard voltage threshold built into the membrane
options.why: there is no sharp threshold anywhere in the equations, only a very steep continuous transition.

options.text: The potassium current, which sets the spike amplitude
options.why: potassium ends the spike; it does not create the all-or-nothing upstroke.

options.text: The refractory period, which prevents partial spikes
options.why: the refractory period limits the *rate* of firing, not the size of an individual spike.

bio.neuro.plasticity-memory.better-at-a-.title: He got better at a task he swore he had never done
bio.neuro.plasticity-memory.better-at-a-.hook: He improved at the task on every attempt, over days, while insisting each time that he had never attempted it.
bio.neuro.plasticity-memory.better-at-a-.author: author-bio-1
bio.neuro.plasticity-memory.better-at-a-.body:
On 1 September 1953 the surgeon William Scoville removed the medial temporal lobes from both sides of a 27-year-old man’s brain. The seizures improved. The patient became the most studied person in the history of neuroscience: Henry Molaison, H.M. in the literature until he died in 2008.

He could hold a conversation and score well on intelligence tests. He could not form new conscious memories. Brenda Milner worked with him for decades and he met her as a stranger every time.

Then she gave him a mirror-drawing task: trace a star seeing only its reflection, which is unnatural and hard. He made roughly thirty errors on his first attempt and five or six by the tenth. The next day he started better than he had finished — and told her, sincerely, that he had never seen it before.

So memory is not one thing. Episodes and facts run through the hippocampus. Skill does not. You can lose your biography and keep your hands.

Twenty years later Bliss and Lømo found a cellular version: a burst of stimulation leaves a synapse stronger for hours — the potentiation Hebb had guessed at in 1949.

recall.question: What did H.M.'s mirror-drawing performance show that his conversation could not?
recall.answer: That skill learning and conscious recollection are separate systems. His hands accumulated practice across days while the hippocampal system that would have let him *remember* practising was gone — so he improved at something he sincerely believed he had never done.

bio.neuro.sleep.nobody-knows-why-you-sle.title: Nobody knows why you sleep
bio.neuro.sleep.nobody-knows-why-you-sle.hook: A third of your life, unconscious and undefended. Evolution rarely pays a bill like that for nothing, and nobody knows what it buys.
bio.neuro.sleep.nobody-knows-why-you-sle.author: author-bio-1
bio.neuro.sleep.nobody-knows-why-you-sle.body:
Every animal anyone has studied closely does something like it, and the cost is outrageous: a third of your life spent immobile, unresponsive, not eating, not watching for anything. Evolution does not usually tolerate a bill that size without a return.

It is also not optional. Rats kept awake die within weeks. Fatal familial insomnia — a prion disease caused by a single letter change in one gene — wrecks the thalamus and kills in about eighteen months, with unstoppable sleeplessness as its leading symptom.

So what is the return? The favourite answer of the last decade was housekeeping. A 2013 paper reported that the space between brain cells expands by around 60% during sleep and that waste proteins wash out about twice as fast. Then in 2024 a group measuring clearance a different way reported the reverse: roughly 30% *less* clearance asleep, 50% less under anaesthesia. Both results are in the literature and the mechanism is unsettled.

What survives: sleep does something for memory and something for metabolism, and you cannot skip it. This is an open problem sitting at the centre of a field rather than at its edge.

recall.question: What is the honest status of the idea that sleep exists to wash waste out of the brain?

options.text: Contested
options.why: the 2013 result has not been withdrawn, but a 2024 study using a different assay found clearance *falls* during sleep, so the mechanism is unresolved.

options.text: Established
options.why: it is the accepted reason animals sleep, confirmed repeatedly since 2013.

options.text: Refuted
options.why: the 2013 finding was retracted and the idea abandoned.

options.text: Irrelevant
options.why: memory consolidation is the only function anyone studies, and clearance was never taken seriously.

bio.neuro.synapses.the-experiment-he-dre.title: The experiment he had to dream twice
bio.neuro.synapses.the-experiment-he-dre.hook: He dreamed the decisive experiment, woke, wrote it down, and in the morning could not read his own handwriting.
bio.neuro.synapses.the-experiment-he-dre.author: author-bio-1
bio.neuro.synapses.the-experiment-he-dre.body:
In 1921 the argument about how one nerve talks to the next was stuck. One camp said electricity jumped the gap. The other said a chemical crossed it, and had no way to show it.

On the night before Easter Sunday, Otto Loewi dreamed the experiment that would settle it. He woke, scribbled it on a scrap of paper by the bed, and went back to sleep. In the morning the note was illegible and he could not reconstruct it. The following night the same dream came back. This time he got dressed and went to the laboratory at three in the morning.

Two frog hearts in saline. Stimulate the vagus nerve on the first and it slows. Take the fluid bathing that heart and pour it over the second heart, which has no nerve attached. The second heart slows too. Something had leaked out of the first one — he called it *Vagusstoff*, "vagus stuff". It turned out to be acetylcholine.

Nobel Prize, 1936.

recall.question: What did the fluid transfer between two frog hearts actually prove?

options.text: That the nerve's effect is carried by a released substance
options.why: a heart with no nerve attached responded to the bathing fluid alone.

options.text: That electrical signals can travel through saline
options.why: an electrical explanation is exactly what the fluid transfer rules out, since no current path existed.

options.text: That the vagus nerve slows the heart
options.why: that was already known; the question was by what means.

options.text: That acetylcholine is the universal transmitter
options.why: Loewi identified an effect, not the molecule, and there turned out to be dozens of transmitters.
